text: We judge ourselves by what we feel capable of doing, while others judge us by what we have already done.
author: Longfellow

text: Every person is responsible for all the good within the scope of his abilities, and for no more.
author: Gail Hamilton

text: The possession of great powers no doubt carries with it a contempt for mere external show.
author: James A. Garfield

text: The art of using moderate abilities to advantage wins praise, and often acquires more reputation than actual brilliancy.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: The measure of capacity is the measure of sphere to either man or woman.
author: Elizabeth Oakes Smith

text: Natural ability can almost compensate for the want of every kind of cultivation; but no cultivation of the mind can make up for the want of natural ability.
author: Schopenhauer

text: An able man shows his spirit by gentle words and resolute actions.
author: Chesterfield

text: No man taketh away sins (which the law, though holy, just and good, could not take away), but He in whom there is no sin.
author: Bede

text: He alone can remit sins who is appointed our Master by the Father of all; He only is able to discern obedience from disobedience.
author: St. Clement of Alexandria

text: It appertaineth to the true God alone to be able to loose men from their sins.
author: St. Cyril

text: Neither angel, nor archangel, nor yet even the Lord Himself (who alone can say "I am with you"), can, when we have sinned, release us, unless we bring repentance with us.
author: St. Ambrose

text: The thing done avails, and not what is said about it.
author: Emerson

text: Action may not always bring happiness; but there is no happiness without action.
author: Beaconsfield

text: To the valiant actions speak alone.
author: Smollett

text: It is well to think well: it is divine to act well.
author: Horace Mann

text: Active natures are rarely melancholy. Activity and melancholy are incompatible.
author: Bovee

text: Trust no Future, howe'er pleasant! Let the dead Past bury its dead! Act, act, in the living Present! Heart within, and God o'erhead!
author: Longfellow

text: Every man feels instinctively that all the beautiful sentiments in the world weigh less than a single lovely action.
author: Lowell

text: Prodigious actions may as well be done By weaver's issue, as by prince's son.
author: Dryden

text: Deliberate with caution, but act with decision; and yield with graciousness, or oppose with firmness.
author: Colton

text: When our souls shall leave this dwelling, the glory of one fair and virtuous action is above all the scutcheons on our tomb, or silken banners over us.
author: J. Shirley

text: Our acts make or mar us,--we are the children of our own deeds.
author: Victor Hugo

text: Man, being essentially active, must find in activity his joy, as well as his beauty and glory; and labor, like everything else that is good, is its own reward.
author: Whipple

text: In the day of prosperity we have many refuges to resort to; in the day of adversity only one.
author: Horatius Bonar

text: Little minds are tamed and subdued by misfortunes; but great minds rise above them.
author: Washington Irving

text: A wretched soul, bruis'd with adversity, We bid be quiet when we hear it cry; But were we burden'd with like weight of pain, As much, or more, we should ourselves complain.
author: Shakespeare

text: Heaven is not always angry when he strikes, But most chastises those whom most he likes.
author: Pomfret

text: The fire of my adversity has purged the mass of my acquaintance.
author: Bolingbroke

text: On every thorn delightful wisdom grows; In every rill a sweet instruction flows.
author: Dr. Young

text: When Providence, for secret ends, Corroding cares, or sharp affliction, sends; We must conclude it best it should be so, And not desponding or impatient grow.
author: Pomfret

text: Adversity has the effect of eliciting talents, which, in prosperous circumstances, would have lain dormant.
author: Horace

text: In this wild world the fondest and the best Are the most tried, most troubled and distress'd.
author: Crabbe

text: There is healing in the bitter cup.
author: Southey

text: Prosperity is the blessing of the Old Testament, adversity is the blessing of the New, which carrieth the greater benediction, and the clearer revelation of God's favor.
author: Bacon

text: In all cases of heart-ache, the application of another man's disappointment draws out the pain and allays the irritation.
author: Lytton

text: The brightest crowns that are worn in heaven have been tried and smelted and polished and glorified through the furnace of tribulation.
author: Chapin

text: Genuine morality is preserved only in the school of adversity, and a state of continuous prosperity may easily prove a quicksand to virtue.
author: Schiller

text: Affectation is a greater enemy to the face than the small-pox.
author: St. Evremond

text: All affectation is the vain and ridiculous attempt of poverty to appear rich.
author: Lavater

text: Affectation hides three times as many virtues as charity does sins.
author: Horace Mann

text: A loving heart is the truest wisdom.
author: Dickens

text: Caresses, expressions of one sort or another, are necessary to the life of the affections as leaves are to the life of a tree. If they are wholly restrained love will die at the roots.
author: Hawthorne

text: Of all earthly music, that which reaches the farthest into heaven is the beating of a loving heart.
author: Beecher

text: If there is anything that keeps the mind open to angel visits, and repels the ministry of ill, it is human love.
author: Willis

text: God sometimes washes the eyes of his children with tears in order that they may read aright His providence and His commandments.
author: T.L. Cuyler

text: The truest help we can render an afflicted man is not to take his burden from him, but to call out his best energy, that he may be able to bear the burden.
author: Phillips Brooks

text: Every man deems that he has precisely the trials and temptations which are the hardest of all for him to bear; but they are so, because they are the very ones he needs.
author: Richter

text: Affliction is but the shadow of God's wing.
author: George Macdonald

text: Aromatic plants bestow No spicy fragrance where they grow; But crushed and trodden to the ground, Diffuse their balmy sweets around.
author: Goldsmith

text: If you would not have affliction visit you twice, listen at once to what it teaches.
author: Burgh

text: Affliction is the wholesome soul of virtue; Where patience, honor, sweet humanity, Calm fortitude, take root, and strongly flourish.
author: Mallet and Thomson

text: Affliction's sons are brothers in distress; A brother to relieve, how exquisite the bliss!
author: Burns

text: With the wind of tribulation God separates in the floor of the soul, the chaff from the corn.
author: Molinos

text: No wise man ever wished to be younger.
author: Swift

text: It is only necessary to grow old to become more indulgent. I see no fault committed that I have not committed myself.
author: Goethe

text: That which is usually called dotage is not the weak point of all old men, but only of such as are distinguished by their levity.
author: Cicero

text: We must not take the faults of our youth into our old age; for old age brings with it its own defects.
author: Goethe

text: Learn to live well, or fairly make your will; You've play'd, and lov'd, and ate, and drank your fill; Walk sober off, before a sprightlier age Comes titt'ring on, and shoves you from the stage.
author: Pope

text: If wrinkles must be written upon our brows, let them not be written upon the heart. The spirit should not grow old.
author: James A. Garfield

text: Forty is the old age of youth; fifty is the youth of old age.
author: Victor Hugo

text: Begin to patch up thine old body for heaven.
author: Shakespeare

text: Few people know how to be old.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: When men grow virtuous in their old age, they are merely making a sacrifice to God of the devil's leavings.
author: Swift

text: The defects of the mind, like those of the countenance, increase with age.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: He who would pass the declining years of his life with honor and comfort, should when young, consider that he may one day become old, and remember, when he is old, that he has once been young.
author: Addison

text: Winter, which strips the leaves from around us, makes us see the distant regions they formerly concealed; so does old age rob us of our enjoyments, only to enlarge the prospect of eternity before us.
author: Richter

text: The easiest thing for our friends to discover in us, and the hardest thing for us to discover in ourselves, is that we are growing old.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: Most people would succeed in small things if they were not troubled with great ambitions.
author: Longfellow

text: He who ascends to mountain tops, shall find The loftiest peaks most wrapt in clouds and snow; He who surpasses or subdues mankind, Must look down on the hate of those below.
author: Southey

text: They that stand high, have many blasts to shake them; And if they fall, they dash themselves to pieces.
author: Shakespeare

text: The path of glory leads but to the grave.
author: Gray

text: We should be careful to deserve a good reputation by doing well; and when that care is once taken, not to be over anxious about the success.
author: Rochester

text: I charge thee, fling away ambition: By that sin fell the angels.
author: Shakespeare

text: Ambition has but one reward for all: A little power, a little transient fame, A grave to rest in, and a fading name!
author: William Winter

text: All my ambition is, I own, To profit and to please unknown; Like streams supplied from springs below, Which scatter blessings as they go.
author: Dr. Cotton

text: If you woo the company of the angels in your waking hours, they will be sure to come to you in your sleep.
author: G.D. Prentice

text: The accusing spirit, which flew up to heaven's chancery with the oath, blushed as he gave it in; and the recording angel, as he wrote it down, dropped a tear upon the word and blotted it out forever.
author: Sterne

text: Millions of spiritual creatures walk the earth Unseen, both when we wake and when we sleep.
author: Milton

text: And to be wroth with one we love Doth work like madness in the brain.
author: Coleridge

text: When anger rushes unrestrain'd to action, Like a hot steed, it stumbles in its way.
author: Savage

text: Lamentation is the only musician that always, like a screech-owl, alights and sits on the roof of an angry man.
author: Plutarch

text: He is a fool who cannot be angry; but he is a wise man who will not.
author: Seneca

text: Men in rage strike those that wish them best.
author: Shakespeare

text: Men often make up in wrath what they want in reason.
author: W.R. Alger

text: Anger is the most impotent passion that accompanies the mind of man; it effects nothing it goes about; and hurts the man who is possessed by it more than any other against whom it is directed.
author: Clarendon

text: When angry, count ten before you speak; if very angry, a hundred.
author: Jefferson

text: An angry man opens his mouth and shuts up his eyes.
author: Cato

text: When a man is wrong and won't admit it, he always gets angry.
author: Haliburton

text: Anger begins with folly and ends with repentance.
author: Pythagoras

text: Anger causes us often to condemn in one what we approve of in another.
author: Pasquier Quesnel

text: Better to be despised for too anxious apprehensions than ruined by too confident a security.
author: Burke

text: Can your solicitude alter the cause or unravel the intricacy of human events?
author: Blair

text: Nothing in life is more remarkable than the unnecessary anxiety which we endure and generally occasion ourselves.
author: Beaconsfield

text: The perfection of art is to conceal art.
author: Quintilian

text: Art must anchor in nature, or it is the sport of every breath of folly.
author: Hazlitt

text: Beauty is at once the ultimate principle and the highest aim of art.
author: Goethe

text: Art does not imitate, but interpret.
author: Mazzini

text: Art is the gift of God, and must be used unto his glory.
author: Longfellow

text: He who comes from the kitchen smells of its smoke; he who adheres to a sect has something of its cant; the college air pursues the student, and dry inhumanity him who herds with literary pedants.
author: Lavater

text: He that walketh with wise men shall be wise.
author: Solomon

text: Choose the company of your superiors whenever you can have it.
author: Lord Chesterfield

text: I set it down as a maxim, that it is good for a man to live where he can meet his betters, intellectual and social.
author: Thackeray

text: Keep good company, and you shall be of the number.
author: George Herbert

text: It is best to be with those in time that we hope to be with in eternity.
author: Fuller

text: The contemplation of celestial things will make a man both speak and think more sublimely and magnificently when he descends to human affairs.
author: Cicero

text: An Atheist-laugh's a poor exchange For Deity offended!
author: Burns

text: By night an atheist half believes a God.
author: Young

text: No one is so much alone in the world as a denier of God.
author: Richter

text: When men live as if there were no God, it becomes expedient for them that there should be none; and then they endeavor to persuade themselves so.
author: Tillotson

text: Atheism is the result of ignorance and pride, of strong sense and feeble reasons, of good eating and ill living.
author: Jeremy Collier

text: Atheism can benefit no class of people,--neither the unfortunate, whom it bereaves of hope, nor the prosperous, whose joys it renders insipid.
author: Chateaubriand

text: Self-possession is the backbone of authority.
author: Haliburton

text: Though authority be a stubborn bear, yet he is oft led by the nose with gold.
author: Shakespeare

text: Choose an author as you choose a friend.
author: Earl of Roscommon

text: Twenty to one offend more in writing too much than too little.
author: Roger Ascham

text: He who proposes to be an author should first be a student.
author: Dryden

text: Nothing is so beneficial to a young author as the advice of a man whose judgment stands constitutionally at the freezing-point.
author: Douglas Jerrold

text: No fathers or mothers think their own children ugly; and this self-deceit is yet stronger with respect to the offspring of the mind.
author: Cervantes

text: There are three difficulties in authorship--to write anything worth the publishing, to find honest men to publish it, and to get sensible men to read it.
author: Colton

text: Never write on a subject without having first read yourself full on it; and never read on a subject till you have thought yourself hungry on it.
author: Richter

text: The two most engaging powers of an author are to make new things familiar, and familiar things new.
author: Thackeray

text: To write well is to think well, to feel well, and to render well; it is to possess at once intellect, soul and taste.
author: Buffon

text: Young authors give their brains much exercise and little food.
author: Joubert

text: It is surely very narrow policy that supposes money to be the chief good.
author: Johnson

text: Poverty is in want of much, but avarice of everything.
author: Publius Syrus

text: There are two considerations which always imbitter the heart of an avaricious man--the one is a perpetual thirst after more riches, the other the prospect of leaving what he has already acquired.
author: Fielding

text: O cursed lust of gold: when for thy sake The fool throws up his interest in both worlds, First starved in this, then damn'd in that to come.
author: Blair

text: Many have been ruined by their fortunes; many have escaped ruin by the want of fortune. To obtain it, the great have become little, and the little great.
author: Zimmermann

text: Avarice is the vice of declining years.
author: George Bancroft

text: The avaricious man is like the barren, sandy ground of the desert, which sucks in all the rain and dews with greediness, but yields no fruitful herbs or plants for the benefit of others.
author: Zeno

text: Avarice in old age, is foolish; for what can be more absurd than to increase our provisions for the road, the nearer we approach to our journey's end?
author: Cicero

text: Poverty wants some, luxury many, and avarice all things.
author: Cowley

text: Modesty is the graceful, calm virtue of maturity; bashfulness the charm of vivacious youth.
author: Mary Wollstonecraft

text: Bashfulness is an ornament to youth, but a reproach to old age.
author: Aristotle

text: It is beauty that begins to please, and tenderness that completes the charm.
author: Fontenelle

text: Keats spoke for all time when he said, "A thing of beauty is a joy forever.
author: Thackeray

text: Beauty is an outward gift which is seldom despised except by those to whom it has been refused.
author: Gibbon

text: I pray Thee, O God, that I may be beautiful within.
author: Socrates

text: Happily there exists more than one kind of beauty. There is the beauty of infancy, the beauty of youth, the beauty of maturity, and, believe me, ladies and gentlemen, the beauty of age.
author: G.A. Sala

text: There is no beauty on earth which exceeds the natural loveliness of woman.
author: J. Petit-Senn

text: There is a self-evident axiom, that she who is born a beauty is half married.
author: Ouida

text: Beauty attracts us men, but if, like an armed magnet it is pointed with gold or silver beside, it attracts with tenfold power.
author: Richter

text: If thou marry beauty, thou bindest thyself all thy life for that which, perchance, will neither last nor please thee one year.
author: Raleigh

text: It is seldom that beautiful persons are otherwise of great virtue.
author: Bacon

text: The most natural beauty in the world is honesty and moral truth.
author: Shaftesbury

text: Every year of my life I grow more convinced that it is wisest and best to fix our attention on the beautiful and good and dwell as little as possible on the dark and the base.
author: Cecil

text: A woman possessing nothing but outward advantages is like a flower without fragrance, a tree without fruit.
author: Regnier

text: All orators are dumb, when beauty pleadeth.
author: Shakespeare

text: Good nature will always supply the absence of beauty; but beauty cannot supply the absence of good nature.
author: Addison

text: There should be, methinks, as little merit in loving a woman for her beauty as in loving a man for his prosperity; both being equally subject to change.
author: Pope

text: Every charitable act is a stepping stone toward heaven.
author: Beecher

text: The disposition to give a cup of cold water to a disciple is a far nobler property than the finest intellect. Satan has a fine intellect but not the image of God.
author: Howells

text: God will excuse our prayers for ourselves whenever we are prevented from them by being occupied in such good works as to entitle us to the prayers of others.
author: Colton

text: The lower a man descends in his love, the higher he lifts his life.
author: W.R. Alger

text: You will find people ready enough to do the Samaritan without the oil and twopence.
author: Sydney Smith

text: Genuine benevolence is not stationary, but peripatetic. It _goeth_ about doing good.
author: Nevins

text: The only way to be loved, is to be and to appear lovely; to possess and display kindness, benevolence, tenderness; to be free from selfishness and to be alive to the welfare of others.
author: Jay

text: The lessons of prudence have charms, And slighted, may lead to distress; But the man whom benevolence warms Is an angel who lives but to bless.
author: Bloomfield

text: The Bible begins gloriously with Paradise, the symbol of youth, and ends with the everlasting kingdom, with the holy city. The history of every man should be a Bible.
author: Novalis

text: The Scriptures teach us the best way of living, the noblest way of suffering, and the most comfortable way of dying.
author: Flavel

text: Like the needle to the North Pole, the Bible points to heaven.
author: R.B. Nichol

text: Whence but from Heaven, could men unskill'd in arts, In several ages born, in several parts, Weave such agreeing truths? or how, or why Should all conspire to cheat us with a lie?
author: Dryden

text: Good, the more communicated, more abundant grows.
author: Milton

text: It has God for its author, salvation for its end, and truth, without any mixture of error, for its matter: it is all pure, all sincere, nothing too much, nothing wanting.
author: Locke

text: A Bible and a newspaper in every house, a good school in every district--all studied and appreciated as they merit--are the principal support of virtue, morality and civil liberty.
author: Franklin

text: Here there is milk for babes, whilst there is manna for angels; truth level with the mind of a peasant; truth soaring beyond the reach of a seraph.
author: Rev. Hugh Stowell

text: All looks yellow to the jaundiced eye.
author: Pope

text: Bigotry dwarfs the soul by shutting out the truth.
author: Chapin

text: A man must be excessively stupid, as well as uncharitable, who believes there is no virtue but on his own side.
author: Addison

text: Show me the man who would go to heaven alone if he could, and in that man I will show you one who will never be admitted into heaven.
author: Feltham

text: The great lesson of biography is to show what man can be and do at his best. A noble life put fairly on record acts like an inspiration to others.
author: Samuel Smiles

text: To be ignorant of the lives of the most celebrated men of antiquity is to continue in a state of childhood all our days.
author: Plutarch

text: Where there is much pretension, much has been borrowed; nature never pretends.
author: Lavater

text: Where boasting ends, there dignity begins.
author: Young

text: A gentleman that loves to hear himself talk will speak more in a minute than he will stand to in a month.
author: Shakespeare

text: The less people speak of their greatness the more we think of it.
author: Bacon

text: Conceit, more rich in matter than in words, Brags of his substance, not of ornament: They are but beggars that can count their worth.
author: Shakespeare

text: No book can be so good as to be profitable when negligently read.
author: Seneca

text: He who loves not books before he comes to thirty years of age, will hardly love them enough afterward to understand them.
author: Clarendon

text: I like books. I was born and bred among them, and have the easy feeling, when I get in their presence, that a stable-boy has among horses.
author: O.W. Holmes

text: Nothing can supply the place of books. They are cheering or soothing companions in solitude, illness, affliction. The wealth of both continents would not compensate for the good they impart.
author: Channing

text: We should have a glorious conflagration if all who cannot put _fire_ into their works would only consent to put their works into the _fire_.
author: Colton

text: He that studies books alone, will know how things ought to be; and he that studies men will know how things are.
author: Colton

text: It is with books as with men: a very small number play a great part; the rest are confounded with the multitude.
author: Voltaire

text: Brevity is the soul of wit, and tediousness the limbs and outward flourishes.
author: Shakespeare

text: Brevity in writing is what charity is to all other virtues--righteousness is nothing without the one, nor authorship without the other.
author: Sydney Smith

text: If you would be pungent, be brief; for it is with words as with sunbeams--the more they are condensed the deeper they burn.
author: Southey

text: The more an idea is developed the more concise becomes its expression; the more a tree is pruned, the better is the fruit.
author: Alfred Bougeant

text: With vivid words your just conceptions grace, Much truth compressing in a narrow space; Then many shall peruse, but few complain, And envy frown, and critics snarl in vain.
author: Pindar

text: Brevity is the child of silence, and is a credit to its parentage.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: A verse may find him whom a sermon flies.
author: George Herbert

text: When a man has no design but to speak plain truth, he may say a great deal in a very narrow compass.
author: Steele

text: That which is everybody's business is nobody's business.
author: Izaak Walton

text: Formerly when great fortunes were only made in war, war was a business; but now, when great fortunes are only made by business, business is war.
author: Bovee

text: Call on a business man at business times only, and on business, transact your business and go about your business, in order to give him time to finish his business.
author: Duke of Wellington

text: Men of great parts are often unfortunate in the management of public business, because they are apt to go out of the common road by the quickness of their imagination.
author: Swift

text: Not because of any extraordinary talents did he succeed, but because he had a capacity on a level for business and not above it.
author: Tacitus

text: Few people do business well who do nothing else.
author: Chesterfield

text: To carry care to bed is to sleep with a pack on your back.
author: Haliburton

text: Cast all your care on God: that anchor holds.
author: Tennyson

text: Care to our coffin adds a nail, no doubt, And every grin, so merry, draws one out.
author: Dr. Wolcot

text: He who climbs above the cares of this world, and turns his face to his God, has found the sunny side of life.
author: Spurgeon

text: It is a good thing to learn caution by the misfortunes of others.
author: Publius Syrus

text: Vessels large may venture more, But little boats should keep near shore.
author: Benjamin Franklin

text: Caution is the eldest child of wisdom.
author: Victor Hugo

text: All is to be feared where all is to be lost.
author: Byron

text: Few persons have sufficient wisdom to prefer censure which is useful to them to praise which deceives them.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: Censure is the tax a man pays to the public for being eminent.
author: Swift

text: The villain's censure is extorted praise.
author: Pope

text: The great hope of society is individual character.
author: Channing

text: Never does a man portray his own character more vividly than in his manner of portraying another.
author: Richter

text: There are beauties of character which, like the night-blooming cereus, are closed against the glare and turbulence of every-day life, and bloom only in shade and solitude, and beneath the quiet stars.
author: Tuckerman

text: There are many persons of whom it may be said that they have no other possession in the world but their character, and yet they stand as firmly upon it as any crowned king.
author: Samuel Smiles

text: The man that makes a character makes foes.
author: Young

text: Every man has three characters--that which he exhibits, that which he has, and that which he thinks he has.
author: Alphonse Karr

text: The best rules to form a young man are to talk little, to hear much, to reflect alone upon what has passed in company, to distrust one's own opinions, and value others that deserve it.
author: Sir William Temple

text: All men are like in their lower natures; it is in their higher characters that they differ.
author: Bovee

text: You may depend upon it that he is a good man whose intimate friends are all good.
author: Lavater

text: Give me the character and I will forecast the event. Character, it has in substance been said, is "victory organized.
author: Bovee

text: Actions, looks, words, steps, form the alphabet by which you may spell characters.
author: Lavater

text: The spirit of the world encloses four kinds of spirits, diametrically opposed to charity--the spirit of resentment, spirit of aversion, spirit of jealousy, and the spirit of indifference.
author: Bossuet

text: Posthumous charities are the very essence of selfishness, when bequeathed by those who, when alive, would part with nothing.
author: Colton

text: The drying up a single tear has more Of honest fame, than shedding seas of gore.
author: Byron

text: Be charitable and indulgent to every one but yourself.
author: Joubert

text: As every lord giveth a certain livery to his servants, charity is the very livery of Christ. Our Saviour, who is the Lord above all lords, would have his servants known by their badge, which is love.
author: Latimer

text: You must have a genius for charity as well as for anything else.
author: Thoreau

text: Prayer carries us half way to God, fasting brings us to the door of his palace, and alms-giving procures us admission.
author: Koran

text: Alas for the rarity of Christian charity under the sun!
author: Hood

text: You cannot separate charity and religion.
author: Colton

text: We should give as we would receive, cheerfully, quickly, and without hesitation; for there is no grace in a benefit that sticks to the fingers.
author: Seneca

text: As the purse is emptied the heart is filled.
author: Victor Hugo

text: Then gently scan your brother man, Still gentler, sister woman; Though they may gang a kennin' wrang, To step aside is human.
author: Burns

text: Cheerfulness is full of significance: it suggests good health, a clear conscience, and a soul at peace with all human nature.
author: Charles Kingsley

text: The mind that is cheerful in its present state, will be averse to all solicitude as to the future, and will meet the bitter occurrences of life with a placid smile.
author: Horace

text: An ounce of cheerfulness is worth a pound of sadness to serve God with.
author: Fuller

text: If good people would but make their goodness agreeable, and smile instead of frowning in their virtue, how many would they win to the good cause!
author: Archbishop Usher

text: Between levity and cheerfulness there is a wide distinction; and the mind which is most open to levity is frequently a stranger to cheerfulness.
author: Blair

text: Inner sunshine warms not only the heart of the owner, but all who come in contact with it.
author: J.T. Fields

text: The way to cheerfulness is to keep our bodies in exercise and our minds at ease.
author: Steele

text: Let us be of good cheer, remembering that the misfortunes hardest to bear are those which never happen.
author: Lowell

text: I love these little people; and it is not a slight thing when they, who are so fresh from God, love us.
author: Dickens

text: The child is father of the man.
author: Wordsworth

text: The smallest children are nearest to God, as the smallest planets are nearest the sun.
author: Richter

author: Stoddard

author: Douglas Jerrold

text: Many children, many cares; no children, no felicity.
author: Bovee

author: Beecher

author: Longfellow

author: Edward Eggleston

text: Where children are there is the golden age.

author: Decker

author: Napoleon I

text: In His death He is a sacrifice, satisfying for our sins; in the resurrection, a conqueror; in the ascension, a king; in the intercession, a high priest.
author: Luther

text: Jesus Christ was more than man.

author: Rousseau

text: A Christian is God Almighty's gentleman.
author: Hare

author: Mrs. John Sanford

text: I desire no other evidence of the truth of Christianity than the Lord's Prayer.
author: Madame de Stael

author: Addison

author: Shakespeare

author: Charron

author: Madame de Girardin

author: Lavater

text: The integrity of men is to be measured by their conduct, not by their professions.
author: Junius

author: Shakespeare

text: A man, like a watch, is to be valued for his manner of going.
author: William Penn

author: Joanna Baillie

author: Milton

author: Hare

author: Auerbach

text: Trust him little who praises all, him less who censures all, and him least who is indifferent about all.
author: Lavater

author: Crabbe

author: Franklin

author: South

author: Joseph Cook

author: South

text: Rules of society are nothing, one's conscience is the umpire.
author: Madame Dudevant

author: Douglas Jerrold

text: In matters of conscience first thoughts are best; in matters of prudence last thoughts are best
author: Rev. Robert Hall

text: We should have all our communications with men, as in the presence of God; and with God, as in the presence of men.
author: Colton

author: Luther

author: Hosea Ballou

author: Sterne

author: Fuller

author: Byron

author: Jeremy Taylor

author: Byrd

author: Condorcet

author: Bovee

author: Balguy

text: The devil does not tempt people whom he finds suitably employed.
author: Jeremy Taylor

text: Employment, which Galen calls "nature's physician," is so essential to human happiness, that indolence is justly considered as the mother of misery.
author: Burton

text: Enthusiasm is the height of man; it is the passing from the human to the divine.
author: Emerson

text: Every production of genius must be the production of enthusiasm.
author: Beaconsfield

text: Let us recognize the beauty and power of true enthusiasm; and whatever we may do to enlighten ourselves and others, guard against checking or chilling a single earnest sentiment.
author: Tuckerman

text: Nothing is so contagious as enthusiasm; it moves stones, it charms brutes. Enthusiasm is the genius of sincerity, and truth accomplishes no victories without it.
author: Lytton

text: Every great and commanding movement in the annals of the world is the triumph of enthusiasm.
author: Emerson

text: The most enthusiastic man in a cause is rarely chosen as a leader.
author: Arthur Helps

text: There is not a passion so strongly rooted in the human heart as envy.
author: Sheridan

text: As a moth gnaws a garment, so doth envy consume a man.
author: St. Chrysostom

text: We ought to be guarded against every appearance of envy, as a passion that always implies inferiority wherever it resides.
author: Pliny

text: Base envy withers at another's joy, And hates that excellence it cannot reach.
author: Thomson

text: The truest mark of being born with great qualities is being born without envy.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: The praise of the envious is far less creditable than their censure; they praise only that which they can surpass, but that which surpasses them they censure.
author: Colton

text: Stones and sticks are thrown only at fruit-bearing trees.
author: Saadi

text: Emulation looks out for merits, that she may exalt herself by a victory; envy spies out blemishes, that she may lower another by a defeat.
author: Colton

text: Envy is a passion so full of cowardice and shame, that nobody ever had the confidence to own it.
author: Rochester

text: Eternity has no gray hairs! The flowers fade, the heart withers, man grows old and dies, the world lies down in the sepulchre of ages, but time writes no wrinkles on the brow of eternity.
author: Bishop Heber

text: If people would but provide for eternity with the same solicitude and real care as they do for this life, they could not fail of heaven.
author: Tillotson

text: The doing an evil to avoid an evil cannot be good.
author: Coleridge

text: The evil that men do lives after them; The good is oft interred with their bones.
author: Shakespeare

text: Evil is wrought by want of thought, As well as want of heart.
author: Hood

text: To overcome evil with good is good, to resist evil with evil is evil.
author: Mohammed

text: We cannot do evil to others without doing it to ourselves.
author: Desmahis

text: If you do what you should not, you must bear what you would not.
author: Franklin

text: As sure as God is good, so surely there is no such thing as necessary evil.
author: Southey

text: In the history of man it has been very generally the case that when evils have grown insufferable they have touched the point of cure.
author: Chapin

text: Example is more forcible than precept. People look at my six days in the week to see what I mean on the seventh.
author: Rev. R. Cecil

text: People seldom improve when they have no other model but themselves to copy after.
author: Goldsmith

text: None preaches better than the ant, and she says nothing.
author: Franklin

text: No reproof or denunciation is so potent as the silent influence of a good example.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: I am satisfied that we are less convinced by what we hear than by what we see.
author: Herodotus

text: Advice may be wrong, but examples prove themselves.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: Example is contagious behavior.
author: Charles Reade

text: The best teachers of humanity are the lives of great men.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: Excess always carries its own retribution.
author: Ouida

text: The misfortune is, that when man has found honey, he enters upon the feast with an appetite so voracious, that he usually destroys his own delight by excess and satiety.
author: Knox

text: The excesses of our youth are drafts upon our old age, payable with interest, about thirty years after date.
author: Colton

text: The body oppressed by excesses, bears down the mind, and depresses to the earth any portion of the divine spirit we had been endowed with.
author: Horace

text: Every morsel to a satisfied hunger is only a new labor to a tired digestion.
author: South

text: Let pleasure be ever so innocent, the excess is always criminal.
author: St. Evremond

text: A man must often exercise or fast or take physic, or be sick.
author: Sir W. Temple

text: It is exercise alone that supports the spirits, and keeps the mind in vigor.
author: Cicero

text: There are many troubles which you cannot cure by the Bible and the hymn-book, but which you can cure by a good perspiration and a breath of fresh air.
author: Beecher

text: Exercise is the chief source of improvement in all our faculties.
author: Blair

text: You will never live to my age without you keep yourself in breath with exercise.
author: Sir P. Sidney

text: To Truth's house there is a single door, which is experience.
author: Bayard Taylor

text: Experience join'd with common sense, To mortals is a providence.
author: Green

text: Experience does take dreadfully high school-wages, but he teaches like no other.
author: Carlyle

text: Experience is a grindstone; and it is lucky for us if we can get brightened by it, and not ground.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: It may serve as a comfort to us in all our calamities and afflictions that he that loses anything and gets wisdom by it is a gainer by the loss.
author: L'Estrange

text: To wilful men, The injuries that they themselves procure, Must be their schoolmasters.
author: Shakespeare

text: Experience keeps a dear school, but fools will learn in no other, and scarce in that; for it is true we may give advice, but we cannot give conduct.
author: Franklin

text: All is but lip wisdom which wants experience.
author: Sir P. Sidney

text: He who is extravagant will quickly become poor; and poverty will enforce dependence, and invite corruption.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: The man who builds, and wants wherewith to pay, Provides a home from which to run away.
author: Young

text: Faith is the key that unlocks the cabinet of God's treasures; the king's messenger from the celestial world, to bring all the supplies we need out of the fullness that there is in Christ.
author: J. Stephens

text: Faith builds a bridge from this world to the next.
author: Young

text: It is impossible to be a hero in anything unless one is first a hero in faith.
author: Jacobi

text: Faith is the root of all good works. A root that produces nothing is dead.
author: Bishop Wilson

text: The person who has a firm trust in the Supreme Being is powerful in his power, wise by his wisdom, happy by his happiness.
author: Addison

text: No cloud can overshadow a true Christian but his faith will discern a rainbow in it.
author: Bishop Horne

text: Faith in God, faith in man, faith in work: this is the short formula in which we may sum up the teachings of the founders of New England,--a creed ample enough for this life and the next.
author: Lowell

text: None despise fame more heartily than those who have no possible claim to it.
author: J. Petit-Senn

text: He who would acquire fame must not show himself afraid of censure. The dread of censure is the death of genius.
author: Simms

text: Though fame is smoke, its fumes are frankincense to human thoughts.
author: Byron

text: He lives in fame that died in virtue's cause.
author: Shakespeare

text: Fame usually comes to those who are thinking about something else,--very rarely to those who say to themselves, "Go to, now let us be a celebrated individual!
author: Holmes

text: The way to fame is like the way to heaven--through much tribulation.
author: Sterne

text: Nor fame I slight, nor for her favors call: She comes unlook'd for, if she comes at all.
author: Pope

text: Write your name in kindness, love and mercy on the hearts of the thousands you come in contact with year by year, and you will never be forgotten.
author: Chalmers

text: Fashion's smile has given wit to dullness and grace to deformity, and has brought everything into vogue, by turns, except virtue.
author: Colton

text: A woman would be in despair if Nature had formed her as fashion makes her appear.
author: Mlle. de L'Espinasse

text: Fashion is among the last influences under which a human being who respects himself, or who comprehends the great end of life, would desire to be placed.
author: Channing

text: The Empress of France had but to change the position of a ribbon to set all the ribbons in Christendom to rustling. A single word from her convulsed the whalebone market of the world.
author: J.G. Holland

text: A fashionable woman is always in love--with herself.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: Change of fashions is the tax which industry imposes on the vanity of the rich.
author: Chamfort

text: Fashion, a word which knaves and fools may use Their knavery and folly to excuse.
author: Churchill

text: O, fear not in a world like this, And thou shalt know ere long,-- Know how sublime a thing it is To suffer and be strong.
author: Longfellow

text: Fear not the proud and the haughty; fear rather him who fears God.
author: Saadi

text: The fear of God is freedom, joy, and peace; And makes all ills that vex us here to cease.
author: Waller

text: Fear is implanted in us as a preservative from evil.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: Fear is the tax that conscience pays to guilt.
author: George Sewell

text: To God, thy country, and thy friend be true.
author: Vaughan

text: He who is faithful over a few things is a lord of cities. It does not matter whether you preach in Westminster Abbey or teach a ragged class, so you be faithful. The faithfulness is all.
author: George Macdonald

text: His words are bonds, his oaths are oracles; His love sincere, his thoughts immaculate; His tears, pure messengers sent from his heart; His heart as far from fraud as heaven from earth.
author: Shakespeare

text: Nothing is more noble, nothing more venerable than fidelity. Faithfulness and truth are the most sacred excellences and endowments of the human mind.
author: Cicero

text: Those are generally good at flattering who are good for nothing else.
author: South

text: If any man flatters me, I'll flatter him again, though he were my best friend.
author: Franklin

text: A man who flatters a woman hopes either to find her a fool or to make her one.
author: Richardson

text: Flatterers are the worst kind of enemies.
author: Tacitus

text: It is better to fall among crows than flatterers; for those devour the dead only, these the living.
author: Antisthenes

text: Nothing is so great an instance of ill-manners as flattery.
author: Swift

text: Men find it more easy to flatter than to praise.
author: Jean Paul

text: 'Tis an old maxim in the schools, That flattery's the food of fools; Yet now and then your men of wit Will condescend to take a bit.
author: Swift

text: Ah! when the means are gone, that buy this praise, The breath is gone whereof this praise is made.
author: Shakespeare

text: Flattery is false money, which would not be current were it not for our vanity.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: Who flatters is of all mankind the lowest, Save he who courts the flattery.
author: Hannah More

text: Men are like stone jugs,--you may lug them where you like by the ears.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: Commend a fool for his wit and a knave for his honesty, and they will receive you into their bosoms.
author: Fielding

text: Flowers are the sweetest things that God ever made and forgot to put a soul into.
author: Beecher

text: In Eastern lands they talk in flowers, And they tell in a garland their loves and cares: Each blossom that blooms in their garden bowers On its leaves a mystic language bears.
author: Percival

text: How the universal heart of man blesses flowers! They are wreathed round the cradle, the marriage altar, and the tomb.
author: Mrs. L.M. Child

text: There is not the least flower but seems to hold up its head and to look pleasantly, in the secret sense of the goodness of its Heavenly Maker.
author: South

text: Flowers knew how to preach divinity before men knew how to dissect and botanize them.
author: H.N. Hudson

text: And with childlike credulous affection We behold their tender buds expand; Emblems of our own great resurrection, Emblems of the bright and better land.
author: Longfellow

text: He who provides for this life, but takes no care for eternity, is wise for a moment, but a fool forever.
author: Tillotson

text: People are never so near playing the fool as when they think themselves wise.
author: Lady Montagu

text: To pardon those absurdities in ourselves which we cannot suffer in others is neither better nor worse than to be more willing to be fools ourselves than to have others so.
author: Pope

text: Surely he is not a fool that hath unwise thoughts, but he that utters them.
author: Bishop Hall

text: It would be easier to endow a fool with intellect than to persuade him that he had none.
author: Babinet

text: It is the peculiar quality of a fool to perceive the faults of others, and to forget his own.
author: Cicero

text: Fools rush in where angels fear to tread.
author: Pope

text: A fool is often as dangerous to deal with as a knave, and always more incorrigible.
author: Colton

text: Young men think old men are fools; but old men know young men are fools.
author: Chapman

text: None but a fool is always right.
author: Hare

text: People have no right to make fools of themselves, unless they have no relations to blush for them.
author: Haliburton

text: Learn from Jesus to love and to forgive. Let the blood of Jesus, which implores pardon for you in heaven, obtain it from you for your brethren here upon earth.
author: Valpy

text: The kindest and the happiest pair Will find occasion to forbear; And something every day they live To pity, and perhaps forgive.
author: Cowper

text: He that cannot forgive others breaks the bridge over which he must pass himself; for every man has need to be forgiven.
author: Lord Herbert

text: They who forgive most shall be most forgiven.
author: Bailey

text: The brave only know how to forgive.
author: Sterne

text: Life, that ever needs forgiveness, has, for its first duty, to forgive.
author: Lytton

text: God's way of forgiving is thorough and hearty,--both to forgive and to forget; and if thine be not so, thou hast no portion of His.
author: Leighton

text: Fortitude implies a firmness and strength of mind, that enables us to do and suffer as we ought. It rises upon an opposition, and, like a river, swells the higher for having its course stopped.
author: Jeremy Collier

text: True fortitude I take to be the quiet possession of a man's self, and an undisturbed doing his duty, whatever evil besets or danger lies in his way.
author: Locke

text: It is a madness to make fortune the mistress of events, because in herself she is nothing, but is ruled by prudence.
author: Dryden

text: The prudent man really frames his own fortunes for himself.
author: Plautus

text: Let fortune do her worst, whatever she makes us lose, so long as she never makes us lose our honesty and our independence.
author: Pope

text: Some are born great, some achieve greatness, and some have greatness thrust upon them.
author: Shakespeare

text: Every man is the architect of his own fortune.
author: Sallust

text: The bad fortune of the good turns their faces up to heaven; and the good fortune of the bad bows their heads down to the earth.
author: Saadi

text: Fortune favors the bold.
author: Cicero

text: I would rather be a freeman among slaves than a slave among freemen.
author: Swift

text: There are two freedoms,--the false, where a man is free to do what he likes; the true, where a man is free to do what he ought.
author: Charles Kingsley

text: The cause of freedom is the cause of God.
author: Bowles

text: And ne'er shall the sons of Columbia be slaves, While the earth bears a plant, or the sea rolls its waves.
author: Robert Treat Paine

text: To have freedom is only to have that which is absolutely necessary to enable us to be what we ought to be, and to possess what we ought to possess.
author: Rahel

text: Freedom is not caprice but room to enlarge.
author: C.A. Bartol

text: The only freedom worth possessing is that which gives enlargement to a people's energy, intellect, and virtues.
author: Channing

text: He was the freeman whom the truth made free; Who first of all, the bands of Satan broke; Who broke the bands of sin, and for his soul, In spite of fools consulted seriously.
author: Pollock

text: Friendship is the only thing in the world concerning the usefulness of which all mankind are agreed.
author: Cicero

text: The man that hails you Tom or Jack, And proves by thumping on your back His sense of your great merit, Is such a friend, that one had need Be very much his friend indeed To pardon or to bear it.
author: Cowper

text: He is a friend indeed who proves himself a friend in need.
author: Plautus

text: There is no man so friendless but that he can find a friend sincere enough to tell him disagreeable truths.
author: Lytton

text: A friendship that makes the least noise is very often the most useful; for which reason I should prefer a prudent friend to a zealous one.
author: Addison

text: No friend's a friend till he shall prove a friend.
author: Beaumont and Fletcher

text: The qualities of your friends will be those of your enemies,--cold friends, cold enemies; half friends, half enemies; fervid enemies, warm friends.
author: Lavater

text: Purchase no friends by gifts; when thou ceasest to give such will cease to love.
author: Fuller

text: The difficulty is not so great to die for a friend as to find a friend worth dying for.
author: Henry Home

text: Real friendship is a slow grower, and never thrives unless engrafted upon a stock of known and reciprocal merit.
author: Chesterfield

text: 'Tis thus that on the choice of friends Our good or evil name depends.
author: Gay

text: We may have many acquaintances, but we can have but few friends; this made Aristotle say that he that hath many friends hath none.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: An act, by which we make one friend and one enemy, is a losing game; because revenge is a much stronger principle than gratitude.
author: Colton

text: That friendship will not continue to the end that is begun for an end.
author: Quarles

text: Be slow to fall into friendship; but when thou art in continue firm and constant.
author: Socrates

text: We cannot expect the deepest friendship unless we are willing to pay the price, a self-sacrificing love.
author: Peloubet

text: False friends are like our shadow, keeping close to us while we walk in the sunshine, but leaving us the instant we cross into the shade.
author: Bovee

text: Be slow in choosing a friend, slower in changing.
author: Franklin

text: The greatest medicine is a true friend.
author: Sir W. Temple

text: True friends visit us in prosperity only when invited, but in adversity they come without invitation.
author: Theophrastus

text: Who friendship with a knave hath made, Is judg'd a partner in the trade.
author: Gay

text: Thou mayest be sure that he who will in private tell thee of thy faults is thy friend, for he adventures thy dislike and doth hazard thy hatred.
author: Sir Walter Raleigh

text: He is happy that hath a true friend at his need; but he is more truly happy that hath no need of his friend.
author: Warwick

text: I would not enter on my list of friends (Though graced with polish'd manners and fine sense, Yet wanting sensibility) the man Who needlessly sets foot upon a worm.
author: Cowper

text: True happiness consists not in the multitude of friends, but in the worth and choice.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: Frugality is founded on the principle that all riches have limits.
author: Burke

text: Frugality may be termed the daughter of prudence, the sister of temperance, and the parent of liberty.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: The world has not yet learned the riches of frugality.
author: Cicero

text: It is vain to be always looking toward the future and never acting toward it.
author: J.F. Boyes

text: The best preparation for the future is the present well seen to, the last duty done.
author: George Macdonald

text: Trust no future howe'er pleasant; Let the dead past bury its dead; Act,--act in the living present, Heart within and God o'erhead!
author: Longfellow

text: The state of that man's mind who feels too intense an interest as to future events, must be most deplorable.
author: Seneca

text: God will not suffer man to have the knowledge of things to come; for if he had prescience of his prosperity, he would be careless; and, understanding of his adversity, he would be senseless.
author: St. Augustine

text: The golden age is not in the past, but in the future; not in the origin of human experience, but in its consummate flower; not opening in Eden, but out from Gethsemane.
author: Chapin

text: How narrow our souls become when absorbed in any present good or ill! it is only the thought of the future that makes them great.
author: Richter

text: If there was no future life, our souls would not thirst for it.
author: Richter

text: Games of chance are traps to catch school boy novices and gaping country squires, who begin with a guinea and end with a mortgage.
author: Cumberland

text: All gaming, since it implies a desire to profit at the expense of another, involves a breach of the tenth commandment.
author: Whately

text: There is but one good throw upon the dice, which is, to throw them away.
author: Chatfield

text: It is the child of avarice, the brother of iniquity and the father of mischief.
author: Washington

text: All my experience of the world teaches me that in ninety-nine cases out of a hundred the safe side and the just side of a question is the generous side and the merciful side.
author: Mrs. Jameson

text: He who gives what he would as readily throw away gives without generosity; for the essence of generosity is in self-sacrifice.
author: Henry Taylor

text: Generosity is only benevolence in practice.
author: Bishop Ken

text: The secret pleasure of a generous act is the great mind's great bribe.
author: Dryden

text: If there be any truer measure of a man than by what he does, it must be by what he gives.
author: South

text: Some are unwisely liberal; and more delight to give presents than to pay debts.
author: Sir P. Sidney

text: When you give, take to yourself no credit for generosity, unless you deny yourself something in order that you may give.
author: Henry Taylor

text: The generous who is always just, and the just who is always generous, may, unannounced, approach the throne of heaven.
author: Lavater

text: Men of the noblest dispositions think themselves happiest when others share their happiness with them.
author: Duncan

text: In giving, a man receives more than he gives; and the more is in proportion to the worth of the thing given.
author: George Macdonald

text: Let us proportion our alms to our ability, lest we provoke God to proportion His blessings to our alms.
author: Beveridge

text: Genius is an immense capacity for taking trouble.
author: Carlyle

text: Genius always gives its best at first, prudence at last.
author: Lavater

text: There is hardly a more common error than that of taking the man who has but one talent for a genius.
author: Helps

text: Talent wears well, genius wears itself out; talent drives a brougham in fact; genius, a sun-chariot in fancy.
author: Ouida

text: Genius unexerted is no more genius than a bushel of acorns is a forest of oaks.
author: Beecher

text: The first and last thing which is required of genius is the love of truth.
author: Goethe

text: Genius can never despise labor.
author: Abel Stevens

text: And genius hath electric power, Which earth can never tame; Bright suns may scorch, and dark clouds lower-- Its flash is still the same.
author: Lydia M. Child

text: Genius must be born, and never can be taught.
author: Dryden

text: Genius is the gold in the mine, talent is the miner who works and brings it out.
author: Lady Blessington

text: One science only will one genius fit; So vast is art, so narrow human wit.
author: Pope

text: I know no such thing as genius,--genius is nothing but labor and diligence.
author: Hogarth

text: Men of genius are often dull and inert in society; as the blazing meteor, when it descends to earth, is only a stone.
author: Longfellow

text: Genius, without religion, is only a lamp on the outer gate of a palace. It may serve to cast a gleam of light on those that are without while the inhabitant sits in darkness.
author: Hannah More

text: Genius is supposed to be a power of producing excellences which are out of the reach of the rules of art: a power which no precepts can teach, and which no industry can acquire.
author: Sir J. Reynolds

text: Propriety of manners, and consideration for others, are the two main characteristics of a gentleman.
author: Beaconsfield

text: Education begins the gentleman, but reading, good company, and reflection must finish him.
author: Locke

text: He is the best gentleman that is the son of his own deserts, and not the degenerated heir of another's virtue.
author: Victor Hugo

text: Perhaps propriety is as near a word as any to denote the manners of the gentleman; elegance is necessary to the fine gentleman; dignity is proper to noblemen; and majesty to kings.
author: Hazlitt

text: Gentleman is a term which does not apply to any station, but to the mind and the feelings in every station.
author: Talfourd

text: Of the offspring of the gentilman Jafeth, came Habraham, Moyses, Aron and the profettys; and also the kyng of the right line of Mary, of whom that gentilman Jhesus was borne.
author: Juliana Berners

text: We do not believe, or we forget, that "the Holy Ghost came down, not in shape of a vulture, but in the form of a dove.
author: Emerson

text: Gentleness in the gait is what simplicity is in the dress. Violent gestures or quick movements inspire involuntary disrespect.
author: Balzac

text: Gentleness, which belongs to virtue, is to be carefully distinguished from the mean spirit of cowards and the fawning assent of sycophants.
author: Blair

text: Give freely to him that deserveth well, and asketh nothing: and that is a way of giving to thyself.
author: Fuller

text: The gift, to be true, must be the flowing of the giver unto me, correspondent to my flowing unto him.
author: Emerson

text: A gift--its kind, its value and appearance; the silence or the pomp that attends it; the style in which it reaches you--may decide the dignity or vulgarity of the giver.
author: Lavater

text: There is no grace in a benefit that sticks to the fingers.
author: Seneca

text: Real glory springs from the quiet conquest of ourselves; and without that the conqueror is nought but the first slave.
author: Thomson

text: The road to glory would cease to be arduous if it were trite and trodden; and great minds must be ready not only to take opportunities but to make them.
author: Colton

text: True glory consists in doing what deserves to be written, in writing what deserves to be read, and in so living as to make the world happier and better for our living in it.
author: Pliny

text: Glory relaxes often and debilitates the mind; censure stimulates and contracts,--both to an extreme. Simple fame is, perhaps, the proper medium.
author: Shenstone

text: I have come to the conclusion that mankind consume twice too much food.
author: Sydney Smith

text: Fat paunches have lean pates; and dainty bits Make rich the ribs, but bankrupt quite the wits.
author: Shakespeare

text: The pleasures of the palate deal with us like Egyptian thieves who strangle those whom they embrace.
author: Seneca

text: God should be the object of all our desires, the end of all our actions, the principle of all our affections, and the governing power of our whole souls.
author: Massillon

text: They that deny a God destroy man's nobility; for certainly man is like the beasts in his body; and if he is not like God in his spirit, he is an ignoble creature.
author: Bacon

text: God is all love; it is He who made everything, and He loves everything that He has made.
author: Henry Brooke

text: How calmly may we commit ourselves to the hands of Him who bears up the world,--of Him who has created, and who provides for the joys even of insects, as carefully as if He were their father.
author: Richter

text: I fear God, and next to God, I chiefly fear him who fears Him not.
author: Saadi

text: A foe to God was never true friend to man.
author: Young

text: God moves in a mysterious way His wonders to perform; He plants His footsteps in the sea, And rides upon the storm.
author: Cowper

text: Who guides below, and rules above, The great disposer, and the mighty king; Than He none greater, next Him none, That can be, is, or was.
author: Horace

text: From God derived, to God by nature join'd. We act the dictates of His mighty mind: And though the priests are mute and temples still, God never wants a voice to speak His will.
author: Rowe

text: It is a most unhappy state to be at a distance with God: man needs no greater infelicity than to be left to himself.
author: Feltham

text: The man who forgets the wonders and mercies of the Lord is without any excuse; for we are continually surrounded with objects which may serve to bring the power and goodness of God strikingly to mind.
author: Slade

text: God is the light which, never seen itself, makes all things visible, and clothes itself in colors. Thine eye feels not its ray, but thine heart feels its warmth.
author: Richter

text: Angels of life and death alike are His; Without His leave they pass no threshold o'er; Who, then, would wish or dare, believing this, Against His messengers to shut the door?
author: Longfellow

text: Gold, like the sun, which melts wax and hardens clay, expands great souls and contracts bad hearts.
author: Rivarol

text: There are two metals, one of which is omnipotent in the cabinet, and the other in the camp,--gold and iron. He that knows how to apply them both may indeed attain the highest station.
author: Colton

text: Trifles light as air Are to the jealous confirmations strong As proofs of holy writ.
author: Shakespeare

text: The very society of joy redoubles it; so that, whilst it lights upon my friend it rebounds upon myself, and the brighter his candle burns the more easily will it light mine.
author: South

text: Who partakes in another's joys is a more humane character than he who partakes in his griefs.
author: Lavater

text: Joy is more divine than sorrow; for joy is bread, and sorrow is medicine.
author: Beecher

text: Without kindness, there can be no true joy.
author: Carlyle

text: Joy is an import; joy is an exchange; Joy flies monopolists: it calls for two; Rich fruit! Heaven planted! never pluck'd by one.
author: Young

text: How are we justly to determine in a world where there are no innocent ones to judge the guilty?
author: Madame de Genlis

text: Who upon earth could live were all judged justly?
author: Byron

text: One man's word is no man's word; we should quietly hear both sides.
author: Goethe

text: Men are not to be judged by their looks, habits, and appearances; but by the character of their lives and conversations, and by their works.
author: L'Estrange

text: The right of private judgment is absolute in every American citizen.
author: James A. Garfield

text: The very thing that men think they have got the most of, they have got the least of; and that is judgment.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: There are no judgments so harsh as those of the erring, the inexperienced, and the young.
author: Miss Mulock

text: The judgment of a great people is often wiser than the wisest men.
author: Kossuth

text: Judge thyself with a judgment of sincerity, and thou wilt judge others with a judgment of charity.
author: Mason

text: 'Tis with our judgments as our watches; none Go just alike, yet each believes his own.
author: Pope

text: Justice offers nothing but what may be accepted with honor; and lays claim to nothing in return but what we ought not even to wish to withhold.
author: Woman'S Rights and Duties

text: Be just and fear not: Let all the ends thou aim'st at be thy country's, Thy God's, and truth's.
author: Shakespeare

text: And heaven that every virtue bears in mind, E'en to the ashes of the just, is kind.
author: Pope

text: He who is only just is cruel.
author: Byron

text: Justice is the insurance which we have on our lives and property, and obedience is the premium which we pay for it.
author: William Penn

text: Heaven is above all yet; there sits a judge that no king can corrupt.
author: Shakespeare

text: Justice discards party, friendship, kindred, and is always, therefore, represented as blind.
author: Addison

text: In matters of equity between man and man, our Saviour has taught us to put my neighbor in place of myself, and myself in place of my neighbor.
author: Dr. Watts

text: The books are balanced in heaven, not here.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: Be just in all thy actions, and if join'd With those that are not, never change thy mind.
author: Denham

text: The virtue of justice consists in moderation, as regulated by wisdom.
author: Aristotle

text: Justice is the great interest of man on earth. It is the ligament which holds civilized beings and civilized nations together.
author: Webster

text: A more glorious victory cannot be gained over another man than this, that when the injury began on his part, the kindness should begin on ours.
author: Tillotson

text: Kindness has converted more sinners than either zeal, eloquence, or learning.
author: F.W. Faber

text: How easy it is for one benevolent being to diffuse pleasure around him; and how truly is a kind heart a fountain of gladness, making everything in its vicinity to freshen into smiles!
author: Washington Irving

text: One kindly deed may turn The fountain of thy soul To love's sweet day-star, that shall o'er thee burn Long as its currents roll.
author: Holmes

text: There is no beautifier of complexion or form or behavior like the wish to scatter joy, and not pain, around us.
author: Emerson

text: A kiss from my mother made me a painter.
author: Benjamin West

text: It is the passion that is in a kiss that gives to it its sweetness; it is the affection in a kiss that sanctifies it.
author: Bovee

text: Four sweet lips, two pure souls, and one undying affection,--these are love's pretty ingredients for a kiss.
author: Bovee

text: You would think, if our lips were made of horn and stuck out a foot or two from our faces, kisses at any rate would be done for. Not so. No creatures kiss each other so much as the birds.
author: Charles Buxton

text: Knowledge is of two kinds. We know a subject ourselves, or we know where we can find information upon it.
author: Boswell

text: If we do not plant knowledge when young, it will give us no shade when we are old.
author: Chesterfield

text: Knowledge is Bought only with a weary care, And wisdom means a world of pain.
author: Joaquin Miller

text: The knowledge which we have acquired ought not to resemble a great shop without order, and without an inventory; we ought to know what we possess, and be able to make it serve us in need.
author: Leibnitz

text: Knowledge is power as well as fame.
author: Rufus Choate

text: Knowledge is leagued with the universe, and findeth a friend in all things; but ignorance is everywhere a stranger, unwelcome; ill at ease and out of place.
author: Tupper

text: Every human being whose mind is not debauched, will be willing to give all that he has to get knowledge.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: If you have knowledge, let others light their candles at it.
author: Fuller

text: Knowledge will not be acquired without pains and application. It is troublesome and deep, digging for pure waters; but when once you come to the spring, they rise up and meet you.
author: Felton

text: Knowledge is proud that he has learned so much; Wisdom is humble that he knows no more.
author: Cowper

text: All wish to possess knowledge, but few, comparatively speaking, are willing to pay the price.
author: Juvenal

text: Seldom ever was any knowledge given to keep, but to impart; the grace of this rich jewel is lost in concealment.
author: Bishop Hall

text: There is no knowledge for which so great a price is paid as a knowledge of the world; and no one ever became an adept in it except at the expense of a hardened or a wounded heart.
author: Lady Blessington

text: Labor is one of the great elements of society,--the great substantial interest on which we all stand.
author: Daniel Webster

text: Hard workers are usually honest. Industry lifts them above temptation.
author: Bovee

text: Bodily labor alleviates the pains of the mind; and hence arises the happiness of the poor.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: Labor disgraces no man; unfortunately, you occasionally find men who disgrace labor.
author: U.S. Grant

text: If the power to do hard work is not talent, it is the best possible substitute for it.
author: James A. Garfield

text: Genius may conceive, but patient labor must consummate.
author: Horace Mann

text: God gives every bird its food, but He does not throw it into the nest. He does not unearth the good that the earth contains, but He puts it in our way, and gives us the means of getting it ourselves.
author: J.G. Holland

text: Labor, wide as the earth, has its summit in heaven.
author: Carlyle

text: Love labor; for if thou dost not want it for food, thou mayest for physic.
author: William Penn

text: Next to faith in God, is faith in labor.
author: Bovee

text: Labor is rest--from the sorrows that greet us; Rest from all petty vexations that meet us, Rest from sin-promptings that ever entreat us, Rest from world-sirens that lure us to ill.
author: Frances S. Osgood

text: No man is born into the world, whose work Is not born with him.
author: Lowell

text: Labor! all labor is noble and holy! Let thy great deeds be thy prayer to thy God.
author: Frances S. Osgood

text: In the commerce of speech use only coin of gold and silver.
author: Joubert

text: The language denotes the man. A coarse or refined character finds its expression naturally in a coarse or refined phraseology.
author: Bovee

text: Language is the picture and counterpart of thought.
author: Mark Hopkins

text: Felicity, not fluency, of language is a merit.
author: Whipple

text: Laughter is a most healthful exertion; it is one of the greatest helps to digestion with which I am acquainted.
author: Dr. Hufeland

text: Men show their character in nothing more clearly than by what they think laughable.
author: Goethe

text: A laugh is worth a hundred groans in any market.
author: Lamb

text: A laugh to be joyous must flow from a joyous heart, for without kindness there can be no true joy.
author: Carlyle

text: One good, hearty laugh is a bombshell exploding in the right place, while spleen and discontent are a gun that kicks over the man who shoots it off.
author: Talmage

text: Stupid people, who do not know how to laugh, are always pompous and self-conceited; that is, ungentle, uncharitable, unchristian.
author: Thackeray

text: Man is the only creature endowed with the power of laughter.
author: Greville

text: Wear your learning like your watch, in a private pocket; and do not pull it out and strike it, merely to show that you have one.
author: Chesterfield

text: He who learns and makes no use of his learning, is a beast of burden, with a load of books.
author: Saadi

text: A little learning is a dangerous thing; Drink deep, or taste not the Pierian spring: There shallow draughts intoxicate the brain, And drinking largely sobers us again.
author: Pope

text: The three foundations of learning: Seeing much, suffering much, and studying much.
author: Catherall

text: The end of learning is to know God, and out of that knowledge to love Him, and to imitate Him, by possessing our souls of true virtue.
author: Milton

text: Learning passes for wisdom among those who want both.
author: Sir W. Temple

text: Learning makes a man fit company for himself.
author: Young

text: He who has no inclination to learn more, will be very apt to think that he knows enough.
author: Powell

text: To be proud of learning is the greatest ignorance.
author: Bishop Taylor

text: Learning is better worth than house or land.
author: Crabbe

text: If you are poor, distinguish yourself by your virtues; if rich, by your good deeds.
author: Joubert

text: He that defers his charity until he is dead is, if a man weighs it rightly, rather liberal of another man's goods than his own.
author: Bacon

text: The God who gave us life gave us liberty at the same time.
author: Thomas Jefferson

text: 'Tis liberty alone that gives the flower Of fleeting life, its lustre and perfume; And we are weeds without it.
author: Cowper

text: The love of liberty that is not a real principle of dutiful behavior to authority is as hypocritical as the religion that is not productive of a good life.
author: Bishop Butler

text: Liberty must be limited in order to be enjoyed.
author: Burke

text: Liberty is from God; liberties, from the devil.
author: Auerbach

text: A day, an hour, of virtuous liberty Is worth a whole eternity in bondage.
author: Addison

text: If liberty with law is fire on the hearth, liberty without law is fire on the floor.
author: Hillard

text: Few persons enjoy real liberty; we are all slaves to ideas or habits.
author: Alfred de Musset

text: Liberty, without wisdom, is license.
author: Burke

text: Life is made up, not of great sacrifices or duties, but of little things, in which smiles and kindness, and small obligations given habitually, are what win and preserve the heart and secure comfort.
author: Sir Humphry Davy

text: Catch, then, O catch the transient hour; Improve each moment as it flies; Life's a short summer--man a flower-- He dies--alas! how soon he dies!
author: Dr. Johnson

text: Life's but a means unto an end, that end, Beginning, mean, and end to all things--God.
author: Bailey

text: In the midst of life we are in death.
author: Church Burial Service

text: Life in itself is neither good nor evil, it is the scene of good or evil, as you make it.
author: Montaigne

text: Since every man who lives is born to die, And none can boast sincere felicity, With equal mind what happens let us bear, Nor joy nor grieve too much for things beyond our care.
author: Dryden

text: Nor love thy life nor hate; but what thou liv'st Live well; how long or short permit to heaven.
author: Milton

text: A handful of good life is worth a bushel of learning.
author: George Herbert

text: Life appears to me too short to be spent in nursing animosity or registering wrongs.
author: Charlotte Bronte

text: That man lives twice that lives the first life well.
author: Herrick

text: He most lives who thinks most, feels the noblest, acts the best; and he whose heart beats the quickest lives the longest.
author: James Martineau

text: Live virtuously, my lord, and you cannot die too soon, nor live too long.
author: Lady Rachel Russell

text: Our life contains a thousand springs, And dies if one be gone; Strange that a harp of thousand strings Should keep in tune so long.
author: Dr. Watts

text: And he that lives to live forever never fears dying.
author: William Penn

text: We live in deeds, not years; in thought, not breaths; In feelings, not in figures on a dial. We should count time by heart-throbs. He most lives, Who thinks most, feels the noblest, acts the best.
author: Bailey

text: The end of life is to be like unto God; and the soul following God, will be like unto Him; He being the beginning, middle, and end of all things.
author: Socrates

text: It matters not how a man dies, but how he lives.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: I slept and dreamed that life was beauty; I woke and found that life was duty.
author: Ellen Sturgis Hooper

text: The truest end of life is to know the life that never ends.
author: William Penn

text: Let those who thoughtfully consider the brevity of life remember the length of eternity.
author: Bishop Ken

text: Hail, holy light! offspring of heaven first-born.
author: Milton

text: Light itself is a great corrective. A thousand wrongs and abuses that are grown in darkness disappear, like owls and bats, before the light of day.
author: James A. Garfield

text: The light in the world comes principally from two sources,--the sun, and the student's lamp.
author: Bovee

text: We never can willingly offend where we sincerely love.
author: Rowland Hill

text: Love and you shall be loved. All love is mathematically just, as much as the two sides of an algebraic equation.
author: Emerson

text: The first symptom of true love in a young man is timidity, in a girl it is boldness. The two sexes have a tendency to approach, and each assumes the qualities of the other.
author: Victor Hugo

text: Love is of all stimulants the most powerful. It sharpens the wits like danger, and the memory like hatred; it spurs the will like ambition; it intoxicates like wine.
author: A.B. Edwards

text: Let those love now who never loved before, Let those that always loved now love the more.
author: Parnell

text: Love rules the court, the camp, the grove, And men below, and saints above; For love is heaven, and heaven is love.
author: Scott

text: Love's like the measles--all the worse when it comes late in life.
author: Jerrold

text: Love's sweetest meanings are unspoken; the full heart knows no rhetoric of words.
author: Bovee

text: A woman is more considerate in affairs of love than a man; because love is more the study and business of her life.
author: Washington Irving

text: It is better to desire than to enjoy, to love than to be loved.
author: Hazlitt

text: Who never loved ne'er suffered; he feels nothing, Who nothing feels but for himself alone.
author: Young

text: Nothing more excites to everything noble and generous, than virtuous love.
author: Henry Home

text: Love, free as air, at sight of human ties, Spreads his light wings, and in a moment flies.
author: Pope

text: But there's nothing half so sweet in life As love's young dream.
author: Moore

text: They do not love, that do not show their love.
author: Shakespeare

text: Love keeps the cold out better than a cloak. It serves for food and raiment.
author: Longfellow

text: That you may be beloved, be amiable.
author: Ovid
