text: All these inconveniences are incidents to love: reproaches, jealousies, quarrels, reconcilements, war, and then peace.
author: Terence

text: Love is a child that talks in broken language, Yet then he speaks most plain.
author: Dryden

text: Love that has nothing but beauty to keep it in good health, is short-lived.
author: Erasmus

text: No cord or cable can draw so forcibly, or bind so fast, as love can do with only a single thread.
author: Burton

text: It is possible that a man can be so changed by love, that one could not recognize him to be the same person.
author: Terence

text: Only those who love with the heart can animate the love of others.
author: Abel Stevens

text: If a man really loves a woman, of course he wouldn't marry her for the world, if he were not quite sure that he was the best person she could by any possibility marry.
author: Holmes

text: True love is humble, thereby is it known; Girded for service, seeking not its own; Vaunts not itself, but speaks in self-dispraise.
author: Abraham Coles

text: Love without faith is as bad as faith without love.
author: Beecher

text: Do you know what a man is? Are not birth, beauty, good shape, discourse, manhood, learning, gentleness, virtue, youth, liberality, and such like, the spice and salt that season a man?
author: Shakespeare

text: A man may twist as he pleases, and do what he pleases, but he inevitably comes back to the track to which nature has destined him.
author: Goethe

text: Men may rise on stepping-stones of their dead selves to higher things.
author: Tennyson

text: It is an error to suppose that a man belongs to himself. No man does. He belongs to his wife, or his children, or his relations, or to his creditors, or to society in some form or other.
author: G.A. Sala

text: How poor, how rich, how abject, how august, How complicate, how wonderful, is man!
author: Young

text: He is the whole encyclopædia of facts. The creation of a thousand forests is in one acorn; and Egypt, Greece, Rome, Gaul, Britain, America, lie folded already in the first man.
author: Emerson

text: Man is an animal that cooks his victuals.
author: Burke

text: Man is an animal that makes bargains; no other animal does this,--one dog does not change a bone with another.
author: Adam Smith

text: Know then thyself, presume not God to scan; The proper study of mankind is man.
author: Pope

text: His life was gentle; and the elements So mix'd in him, that nature might stand up And say to all the world, "This was a man!
author: Shakespeare

text: Make yourself an honest man, and then you may be sure that there is one rascal less in the world.
author: Carlyle

text: An individual man is a fruit which it cost all the foregoing ages to form and ripen. He is strong, not to do, but to live; not in his arms, but in his heart; not as an agent, but as a fact.
author: Emerson

text: What a piece of work is a man! How noble in reason! how infinite in faculties! in form and moving how express and admirable! in action, how like an angel! in apprehension, how like a god!
author: Shakespeare

text: There are but three classes of men, the retrograde, the stationary, and the progressive.
author: Lavater

text: Before man made us citizens, great nature made us men.
author: Lowell

text: The person who screams, or uses the superlative degree, or converses with heat puts whole drawing-rooms to flight. If you wish to be loved, love measure.
author: Emerson

text: Good manners is the art of making those people easy with whom we converse.
author: Swift

text: There is certainly something of exquisite kindness and thoughtful benevolence in that rarest of gifts,--fine breeding.
author: Lytton

text: In the society of ladies, want of sense is not so unpardonable as want of manners.
author: Lavater

text: Good manners are a part of good morals.
author: Whatley

text: One principal part of good breeding is to suit our behavior to the three several degrees of men: our superiors, our equals, and those below us.
author: Swift

text: As a man's salutations, so is the total of his character; in nothing do we lay ourselves so open as in our manner of meeting and salutation.
author: Lavater

text: Grace is to the body what good sense is to the mind.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: Good breeding is the result of much good sense, some good nature, and a little self-denial for the sake of others, and with a view to obtain the same indulgence from them.
author: Chesterfield

text: To be good and disagreeable is high treason against the royalty of virtue.
author: Hannah More

text: A man's own good breeding is the best security against other people's ill manners.
author: Chesterfield

text: I chose my wife, as she did her wedding gown, for qualities that would wear well.
author: Goldsmith

text: A man may be cheerful and contented in celibacy, but I do not think he can ever be happy; it is an unnatural state, and the best feelings of his nature are never called into action.
author: Southey

text: When thou choosest a wife, think not only of thyself, but of those God may give thee of her, that they reproach thee not for their being.
author: Tupper

text: An obedient wife commands her husband.
author: Tennyson

text: No man can either live piously or die righteous without a wife.
author: Richter

text: Man is the circled oak; woman the ivy.
author: Aaron Hill

text: Go down the ladder when thou marriest a wife; go up when thou choosest a friend.
author: Rabbi Ben Azai

text: Though fools spurn Hymen's gentle pow'rs, We who improve his golden hours, By sweet experience know, That marriage, rightly understood, Gives to the tender and the good A paradise below.
author: Cotton

text: As a walled town is more worthier than a village, so is the forehead of a married man more honorable than the bare brow of a bachelor.
author: Shakespeare

text: God the best maker of all marriages.
author: Shakespeare

text: 20. Never let your hopes stop short of the eternal home.
author: Cottager and Artisan

text: Let us no more contend, nor blame Each other, blamed enough elsewhere, but strive In offices of love, how we may lighten Each other's burden, in our share of woe.
author: Milton

text: The world well tried, the sweetest thing in life Is the unclouded welcome of a wife.
author: Willis

text: A wife is a gift bestowed upon a man to reconcile him to the loss of paradise.
author: Goethe

text: Heaven will be no heaven to me if I do not meet my wife there.
author: Andrew Jackson

text: If you wish to ruin yourself, marry a rich wife.
author: Michelet

text: When I said I would die a bachelor, I did not think I should live till I were married.
author: Shakespeare

text: Of earthly goods the best, is a good wife.
author: Simonides

text: Take the daughter of a good mother.
author: Fuller

text: Every effort is made in forming matrimonial alliances to reconcile matters relating to fortune, but very little is paid to the congeniality of dispositions, or to the accordance of hearts.
author: Massillon

text: A married man has many cares, but a bachelor no pleasures.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: Meditation is the soul's perspective glass, whereby, in her long removes, she discerneth God, as if He were near at hand.
author: Feltham

text: Melancholy sees the worst of things,--things as they may be, and not as they are. It looks upon a beautiful face, and sees but a grinning skull.
author: Bovee

text: Let us be merciful as well as just.
author: Longfellow

text: Consider this,-- That, in the course of justice, none of us Should see salvation: we do pray for mercy; And that same prayer doth teach us all to render The deeds of mercy.
author: Shakespeare

text: Among the attributes of God, although they are all equal, mercy shines with even more brilliancy than justice.
author: Cervantes

text: God's mercy is a holy mercy, which knows how to pardon sin, not to protect it; it is a sanctuary for the penitent, not for the presumptuous.
author: Bishop Reynolds

text: It is enthroned in the heart of kings, It is an attribute to God himself; And earthly power doth then show likest God's When mercy seasons justice.
author: Shakespeare

text: Lenity will operate with greater force, in some instances, than rigor. It is therefore my first wish to have my whole conduct distinguished by it.
author: Washington

text: Teach me to feel another's woe, To hide the fault I see; That mercy I to others show, That mercy show to me.
author: Pope

text: Sweet mercy is nobility's true badge.
author: Shakespeare

text: There is merit without elevation, but there is no elevation without some merit.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: On their own merits modest men are dumb.
author: George Colman

text: The mark of extraordinary merit is to see those most envious of it constrained to praise.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: Our minds are like certain vehicles,--when they have little to carry they make much noise about it, but when heavily loaded they run quietly.
author: Elihu Burritt

text: It is the mind that makes the body rich.
author: Shakespeare

text: A weak mind is like a microscope, which magnifies trifling things, but cannot receive great ones.
author: Chesterfield

text: Were I so tall to reach the pole, Or grasp the ocean with my span, I must be measur'd by my soul: The mind's the standard of the man.
author: Dr. Watts

text: The mind is its own place, and in itself Can make a heaven of hell, a hell of heaven.
author: Milton

text: He that has treasures of his own May leave the cottage or the throne, May quit the globe, and dwell alone Within his spacious mind.
author: Dr. Watts

text: The mind grows narrow in proportion as the soul grows corrupt.
author: Rousseau

text: Every great mind seeks to labor for eternity. All men are captivated by immediate advantages; great minds alone are excited by the prospect of distant good.
author: Schiller

text: Mind unemployed is mind unenjoyed.
author: Bovee

text: As the mind must govern the hands, so in every society the man of intelligence must direct the man of labor.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: As the soil, however rich it may be, cannot be productive without culture, so the mind without cultivation can never produce good fruit.
author: Seneca

text: Few minds wear out; more rust out.
author: Bovee

text: Minds of moderate calibre ordinarily condemn everything which is beyond their range.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: Guard well thy thoughts: our thoughts are heard in heaven.
author: Young

text: It is the mind that maketh good or ill, That maketh wretch or happy, rich or poor.
author: Spenser

text: Harmless mirth is the best cordial against the consumption of the spirit; wherefore jesting is not unlawful, if it trespasseth not in quantity, quality, or season.
author: Fuller

text: Care to our coffin adds a nail, no doubt; And ev'ry grin so merry draws one out.
author: Peter Pindar

text: I love such mirth as does not make friends ashamed to look upon one another next morning.
author: Izaak Walton

text: The diamond of character is revealed by the concussion of misfortune, as the splendor of the precious jewel of the mine is developed by the blows of the lapidary.
author: F.A. Durivage

text: A soul exasperated in ills, falls out With everything, its friend, itself.
author: Addison

text: We have all of us sufficient fortitude to bear the misfortunes of others.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: The good man, even though overwhelmed by misfortune, loses never his inborn greatness of soul. Camphor-wood burnt in the fire becomes all the more fragrant.
author: Sataka

text: Who hath not known ill-fortune, never knew Himself, or his own virtue.
author: Mallet

text: Little minds are tamed and subdued by misfortune; but great minds rise above it.
author: Washington Irving

text: When one is past, another care we have; Thus woe succeeds a woe, as wave a wave.
author: Herrick

text: The greatest misfortune of all is not to be able to bear misfortune.
author: Bias

text: I believe, indeed, that it is more laudable to suffer great misfortunes than to do great things.
author: Stanislaus

text: Our bravest lessons are not learned through success, but misadventure.
author: Alcott

text: The less we parade our misfortunes the more sympathy we command.
author: Orville Dewey

text: We should learn, by reflecting on the misfortunes which have attended others, that there is nothing singular in those which befall ourselves.
author: Melmoth

text: Most of our misfortunes are more supportable than the comments of our friends upon them.
author: Colton

text: The mob has nothing to lose, everything to gain.
author: Goethe

text: The mob have neither judgment nor principle,--ready to bawl at night for the reverse of what they desired in the morning.
author: Tacitus

text: The scum that rises upmost, when the nation boils.
author: Dryden

text: The mob is a sort of bear; while your ring is through its nose, it will even dance under your cudgel; but should the ring slip, and you lose your hold, the brute will turn and rend you.
author: Jane Porter

text: Inconstant, blind, Deserting friends at need, and duped by foes; Loud and seditious, when a chief inspired Their headlong fury, but, of him deprived, Already slaves that lick'd the scourging hand.
author: Thomson

text: Let there be an entire abstinence from intoxicating drinks throughout this country during the period of a single generation, and a mob would be as impossible as combustion without oxygen.
author: Horace Mann

text: Unlimited activity, of whatever kind, must end in bankruptcy.
author: Goethe

text: A thing moderately good is not so good as it ought to be. Moderation in temper is always a virtue; but moderation in principle is always a vice.
author: Thomas Paine

text: The boundary of man is moderation. When once we pass that pale our guardian angel quits his charge of us.
author: Feltham

text: Moderation is the silken string running through the pearl chain of all virtues.
author: Bishop Hall

text: The superior man wishes to be slow in his words and earnest in his conduct.
author: Confucius

text: Moderation resembles temperance. We are not unwilling to eat more, but are afraid of doing ourselves harm.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: A modest person seldom fails to gain the goodwill of those he converses with, because nobody envies a man who does not appear to be pleased with himself.
author: Steele

text: Modesty seldom resides in a breast that is not enriched with nobler virtues.
author: Goldsmith

text: True modesty avoids everything that is criminal; false modesty everything that is unfashionable.
author: Addison

text: Modesty once extinguished knows not how to return.
author: Seneca

text: Modesty never rages, never murmurs, never pouts when it is ill-treated.
author: Steele

text: The first of all virtues is innocence; the next is modesty. If we banish modesty out of the world, she carries away with her half the virtue that is in it.
author: Addison

text: God intended for women two preventatives against sin, modesty and remorse; in confession to a mortal priest the former is removed by his absolution, the latter is taken away.
author: Miranda of Piedmont

text: Make all you can, save all you can, give all you can.
author: Wesley

text: What a dignity it gives an old lady, that balance at the bankers! How tenderly we look at her faults if she is a relative; what a kind, good-natured old creature we find her!
author: Thackeray

text: A wise man should have money in his head, but not in his heart.
author: Swift

text: Money is a good servant, but a dangerous master.
author: Bouhours

text: By doing good with his money, a man as it were stamps the image of God upon it, and makes it pass current for the merchandise of heaven.
author: Rutledge

text: The deepest depth of vulgarism is that of setting up money as the ark of the covenant.
author: Carlyle

text: In cases of doubtful morality, it is usual to say, Is there any harm in doing this? This question may sometimes be best answered by asking ourselves another: Is there any harm in letting it alone?
author: Colton

text: To give a man a full knowledge of true morality, I would send him to no other book than the New Testament.
author: Locke

text: Ten men have failed from defect in morals where one has failed from defect in intellect.
author: Horace Mann

text: The moral law is written on the tablets of eternity. For every false word or unrighteous deed, for cruelty and oppression, for lust or vanity, the price has to be paid at last.
author: Froude

text: All sects are different, because they come from men; morality is everywhere the same, because it comes from God.
author: Voltaire

text: The mother in her office holds the key of the soul.
author: Old Play

text: There is a sight all hearts beguiling-- A youthful mother to her infant smiling, Who with spread arms and dancing feet, A cooing voice, returns its answer sweet.
author: Baillie

text: A mother is a mother still, The holiest thing alive.
author: Coleridge

text: If there be aught surpassing human deed or word or thought, it is a mother's love!
author: Marchioness de Spadara

text: I think it must somewhere be written, that the virtues of mothers shall, occasionally, be visited on their children, as well as the sins of fathers.
author: Dickens

text: Unhappy is the man for whom his own mother has not made all other mothers venerable.
author: Richter

text: The instruction received at the mother's knee, and the paternal lessons, together with the pious and sweet souvenirs of the fireside, are never effaced entirely from the soul.
author: Lamennais

text: One good mother is worth a hundred schoolmasters.
author: George Herbert

text: An ounce of mother," says the Spanish proverb, "is worth a pound of clergy.
author: T.W. Higginson

text: Youth fades; love droops; the leaves of friendship fall; A mother's secret hope outlives them all.
author: Holmes

text: All that I am, my mother made me.
author: J.Q. Adams

text: He mourns the dead who lives as they desire.
author: Young

text: Of permanent mourning there is none; no cloud remains fixed. The sun will shine to-morrow.
author: Richter

text: The true way to mourn the dead is to take care of the living who belong to them.
author: Burke

text: No longer mourn for me when I am dead, Than you shall hear the surly sullen bell Give warning to the world that I am fled.
author: Shakespeare

text: Music is the medicine of an afflicted mind, a sweet sad measure is the balm of a wounded spirit; and joy is heightened by exultant strains.
author: Henry Giles

text: Sweet music! sacred tongue of God.
author: Charles G. Leland

text: Music is the fourth great material want of our natures,--first food, then raiment, then shelter, then music.
author: Bovee

text: When griping grief the heart doth wound, And doleful dumps the mind oppress, Then music, with her silver sound, With speedy help doth lend redress.
author: Shakespeare

text: Some of the fathers went so far as to esteem the love of music a sign of predestination; as a thing divine, and reserved for the felicities of heaven itself.
author: Sir W. Temple

text: Music hath charms to soothe a savage breast, To soften rocks, or bend a knotted oak.
author: Congreve

text: There's music in the sighing of a reed; There's music in the gushing of a rill; There's music in all things, if men had ears.
author: Byron

text: The man that hath no music in himself, Nor is not moved with concord of sweet sounds, Is fit for treasons, stratagems, and spoils.
author: Shakespeare

text: O, pleasant is the welcome kiss When day's dull round is o'er; And sweet the music of the step That meets us at the door.
author: J.R. Drake

text: Not the rich viol, trump, cymbal, nor horn, Guitar, nor cittern, nor the pining flute, Are half so sweet as tender human words.
author: Barry Cornwall

text: Is there a heart that music cannot melt? Alas! how is that rugged heart forlorn.
author: Beattie

text: Music cleanses the understanding, inspires it, and lifts it into a realm which it would not reach if it were left to itself.
author: Henry Ward Beecher

text: Music is a discipline, and a mistress of order and good manners; she makes the people milder and gentler, more moral and more reasonable.
author: Luther

text: Amongst the instrumentalities of love and peace, surely there can be no sweeter, softer, more effective voice than that of gentle, peace-breathing music.
author: Elihu Burritt

text: Explain it as we may, a martial strain will urge a man into the front rank of battle sooner than an argument, and a fine anthem excite his devotion more certainly than a logical discourse.
author: Tuckerman

text: Music should strike fire from the heart of man, and bring tears from the eyes of woman.
author: Beethoven

text: Music is the child of prayer, the companion of religion.
author: Chateaubriand

text: Had I children, my utmost endeavors would be to make them musicians.
author: Horace Walpole

text: Next to theology I give to music the highest place and honor. And we see how David and all the saints have wrought their godly thoughts into verse, rhyme, and song.
author: Luther

text: Everything made by man may be destroyed by man; there are no ineffaceable characters except those engraved by nature; and nature makes neither princes nor rich men nor great lords.
author: Rousseau

text: Nature never did betray The heart that loved her.
author: Wordsworth

text: All are but parts of one stupendous whole, Whose body nature is, and God the soul.
author: Pope

text: It is a great mortification to the vanity of man that his utmost art and industry can never equal the meanest of nature's productions, either for beauty or value.
author: Hume

text: Read nature; nature is a friend to truth; Nature is Christian, preaches to mankind; And bids dead matter aid us in our creed.
author: Young

text: Nature ever faithful is To such as trust her faithfulness.
author: Emerson

text: Nature is God's Old Testament.
author: Theodore Parker

text: Nature and wisdom never are at strife.
author: Juvenal

text: You will find something far greater in the woods than you will find in books. Stones and trees will teach you that which you will never learn from masters.
author: St. Bernard

text: He who is lord of himself, and exists upon his own resources, is a noble but a rare being.
author: Sir E. Brydges

text: If a man be endued with a generous mind, this is the best kind of nobility.
author: Plato

text: A noble life crowned with heroic death, rises above and outlives the pride and pomp and glory of the mightiest empire of the earth.
author: James A. Garfield

text: Nature makes all the noblemen; wealth, education, or pedigree never made one yet.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: Be noble! and the nobleness that lives In other men, sleeping, but never dead, Will rise in majesty to meet thine own.
author: Lowell

text: Howe'er it be, it seems to me, 'Tis only noble to be good.
author: Tennyson

text: The virtue of paganism was strength; the virtue of Christianity is obedience.
author: Hare

text: Obedience is not truly performed by the body of him whose heart is dissatisfied. The shell without a kernel is not fit for store.
author: Saadi

text: He praiseth God best that serveth and obeyeth Him most: the life of thankfulness consists in the thankfulness of the life.
author: Burkitt

text: No principle is more noble, as there is none more holy, than that of a true obedience.
author: Henry Giles

text: Obedience, we may remember, is a part of religion, and therefore an element of peace; but love which includes obedience is the whole.
author: George Sewell

text: The virtue of Christianity is obedience.
author: J.C. Hare

text: Prepare thy soul calmly to obey; such offering will be more acceptable to God than every other sacrifice.
author: Metastasio

text: Obstinacy is ever most positive when it is most in the wrong.
author: Madame Necker

text: People first abandon reason, and then become obstinate; and the deeper they are in error the more angry they are.
author: Blair

text: An obstinate man does not hold opinions, but they hold him.
author: Pope

text: Most other passions have their periods of fatigue and rest, their suffering and their cure; but obstinacy has no resource, and the first wound is mortal.
author: Thomas Paine

text: Narrowness of mind is often the cause of obstinacy; we do not easily believe beyond what we see.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: Obstinacy and vehemency in opinion are the surest proofs of stupidity.
author: Barton

text: Cheerfulness is the daughter of employment; and I have known a man come home in high spirits from a funeral, merely because he has had the management of it.
author: Dr. Horne

text: Employment, which Galen calls "nature's physician," is so essential to human happiness that indolence is justly considered as the mother of misery.
author: Burton

text: Occupation alone is happiness.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: The great happiness of life, I find, after all, to consist in the regular discharge of some mechanical duty.
author: Schiller

text: The crowning fortune of a man is to be born to some pursuit which finds him employment and happiness, whether it be to make baskets, or broadswords, or canals, or statues, or songs.
author: Emerson

text: Blessed is he who has found his work; let him ask no other blessedness. He has a work, a life purpose. Labor is life.
author: Carlyle

text: One only "right" we have to assert in common with mankind--and that is as much in our hands as theirs--is the right of having something to do.
author: Miss Mulock

text: Opinions should be formed with great caution, and changed with greater.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: Do not think of knocking out another person's brains because he differs in opinion from you. It would be as rational to knock yourself on the head because you differ from yourself ten years ago.
author: Horace Mann

text: He who has no opinion of his own, but depends upon the opinion and taste of others, is a slave.
author: Klopstock

text: To maintain an opinion because it is thine, and not because it is true, is to prefer thyself above the truth.
author: Venning

text: We should always keep a corner of our heads open and free, that we may make room for the opinions of our friends. Let us have heart and head hospitality.
author: Joubert

text: No liberal man would impute a charge of unsteadiness to another for having changed his opinion.
author: Cicero

text: It is not only arrogant, but it is profligate, for a man to disregard the world's opinion of himself.
author: Cicero

text: In the minds of most men, the kingdom of opinion is divided into three territories,--the territory of yes, the territory of no, and a broad, unexplored middle ground of doubt.
author: James A. Garfield

text: The foolish and the dead alone never change their opinion.
author: Lowell

text: Public opinion, though often formed upon a wrong basis, yet generally has a strong underlying sense of justice.
author: Abraham Lincoln

text: Opportunity is rare, and a wise man will never let it go by him.
author: Bayard Taylor

text: Many do with opportunities as children do at the seashore; they fill their little hands with sand, and then let the grains fall through, one by one, till all are gone.
author: Rev. T. Jones

text: Do not wait for extraordinary circumstances to do good actions; try to use ordinary situations.
author: Richter

text: The best men are not those who have waited for chances, but who have taken them,--besieged the chance, conquered the chance, and made the chance their servitor.
author: Chapin

text: The opportunity to do mischief is found a hundred times a day, and that of doing good once a year.
author: Voltaire

text: There is an hour in each man's life appointed to make his happiness, if then he seize it.
author: Beaumont and Fletcher

text: There is no man whom fortune does not visit once in his life; but when she does not find him ready to receive her, she walks in at the door and flies out at the window.
author: Cardinal Imperiali

text: Nothing is so often irrevocably neglected as an opportunity of daily occurrence.
author: Marie Ebner-Eschenbach

text: Give me a chance, says Stupid, and I will show you. Ten to one he has had his chance already, and neglected it.
author: Haliburton

text: Opportunity has hair in front; behind she is bald. If you seize her by the forelock, you may hold her; but if suffered to escape, not Jupiter himself can catch her again.
author: Seneca

text: He that wrestles with us strengthens our nerves, and sharpens our skill. Our antagonist is our helper.
author: Burke

text: To make a young couple love each other, it is only necessary to oppose and separate them.
author: Goethe

text: Order is heaven's first law.
author: Pope

text: Order is to arrangement what the soul is to the body, and what mind is to matter.
author: Joubert

text: Order is the sanity of the mind, the health of the body, the peace of the city, the security of the State. As the beams to a house, as the bones to the microcosm of man, so is order to all things.
author: Southey

text: The heavens themselves, the planets, and this centre, Observe degree, priority, and place, Insisture, course, proportion, season, form, Office, and custom, in all line of order.
author: Shakespeare

text: Fretfulness of temper will generally characterize those who are negligent of order.
author: Blair

text: Every man has a paradise around him till he sins, and the angel of an accusing conscience drives him from his Eden.
author: Longfellow

text: Gentleness and kindness will make our homes a paradise upon earth.
author: Bartol

text: The sacred books of the ancient Persians say: "If you would be holy instruct your children, because all the good acts they perform will be imputed to you.
author: Montesquieu

text: Of all hardness of heart there is none so inexcusable as that of parents toward their children. An obstinate, inflexible, unforgiving temper is odious upon all occasions; but here it is unnatural.
author: Addison

text: Next to God, thy parents.
author: William Penn

text: Whoever makes his father's heart to bleed, Shall have a child that will revenge the deed.
author: Randolph

text: How pleasant it is for a father to sit at his child's board. It is like the aged man reclining under the shadow of the oak which he has planted.
author: Scot'S Magazine

text: The passions are the gales of life; and it is religion only that can prevent them from rising into a tempest.
author: Dr. Watts

text: Strong as our passions are, they may be starved into submission, and conquered without being killed.
author: Colton

text: The ruling passion, be it what it will, The ruling passion conquers reason still.
author: Pope

text: Men spend their lives in the service of their passions, instead of employing their passions in the service of their lives.
author: Steele

text: Hold not conference, debate, or reasoning with any lust; 'tis but a preparatory for thy admission of it. The way is at the very first flatly to deny it.
author: Fuller

text: In the human breast two master-passions cannot coexist.
author: Campbell

text: Even virtue itself, all perfect as it is, requires to be inspirited by passion; for duties are but coldly performed which are but philosophically fulfilled.
author: Mrs. Jameson

text: Our headstrong passions shut the door of our souls against God.
author: Confucius

text: Men will always act according to their passions. Therefore the best government is that which inspires the nobler passions and destroys the meaner.
author: Jacobi

text: Passion costs too much to bestow it upon every trifle.
author: Rev. Thomas Adam

text: Words may be counterfeit, false coined, and current only from the tongue, without the mind; but passion is in the soul, and always speaks the heart.
author: Southern

text: A genuine passion is like a mountain stream; it admits of no impediment; it cannot go backward; it must go forward.
author: Bovee

text: Passion is the drunkenness of the mind.
author: South

text: Exalted souls Have passions in proportion violent, Resistless, and tormenting; they're a tax Imposed by nature on pre-eminence, And fortitude and wisdom must support them.
author: Lillo

text: One master-passion in the breast, Like Aaron's serpent, swallows up the rest.
author: Pope

text: Oh how the passions, insolent and strong, Bear our weak minds their rapid course along; Make us the madness of their will obey; Then die and leave us to our griefs a prey!
author: Crabbe

text: A great passion has no partner.
author: Lavater

text: When the tongue or the pen is let loose in a frenzy of passion, it is the man, and not the subject, that becomes exhausted.
author: Thomas Paine

text: He who is passionate and hasty is generally honest. It is your cool, dissembling hypocrite of whom you should beware.
author: Lavater

text: The passions are like fire, useful in a thousand ways and dangerous only in one, through their excess.
author: Bovee

text: It is not the absence, but the mastery, of our passions which affords happiness.
author: Mme. de Maintenon

text: The past is utterly indifferent to its worshipers.
author: William Winter

text: Not to know what happened before we were born is always to remain a child; to know, and blindly to adopt that knowledge as an implicit rule of life, is never to be a man.
author: Chatfield

text: No hand can make the clock strike for me the hours that are passed.
author: Byron

text: The present is only intelligible in the light of the past.
author: Trench

text: Study the past if you would divine the future.
author: Confucius

text: The best of prophets of the future is the past.
author: Byron

text: Some are so very studious of learning what was done by the ancients that they know not how to live with the moderns.
author: William Penn

text: The past and future are veiled; but the past wears the widow's veil; the future, the virgin's.
author: Richter

text: He that can have patience can have what he will.
author: Franklin

text: Our real blessings often appear to us in the shape of pains, losses and disappointments; but let us have patience, and we soon shall see them in their proper figures.
author: Addison

text: Never think that God's delays are God's denials. Hold on; hold fast; hold out. Patience is genius.
author: Buffon

text: There is, however, a limit at which forbearance ceases to be a virtue.
author: Burke

text: We usually learn to wait only when we have no longer anything to wait for.
author: Marie Ebner-Eschenbach

text: No school is more necessary to children than patience, because either the will must be broken in childhood or the heart in old age.
author: Richter

text: He that will have a cake of the wheat must needs tarry the grinding.
author: Shakespeare

text: Patience is a nobler motion than any deed.
author: C.A. Bartol

text: Patience is the support of weakness; impatience is the ruin of strength.
author: Colton

text: If the wicked flourish and thou suffer, be not discouraged. They are fatted for destruction; thou art dieted for health.
author: Fuller

text: Patience is sorrow's salve.
author: Churchill

text: He serves his party best, who serves the country best.
author: Rutherford B. Hayes

text: Be just, and fear not; Let all the ends thou aim'st at, be thy country's, Thy God's, and Truth's.
author: Shakespeare

text: Such is the patriot's boast, where'er we roam, His first, best country ever is at home.
author: Goldsmith

text: I love my country's good, with a respect more tender, more holy and profound, than my own life.
author: Shakespeare

text: Strike--for your altars and your fires; Strike--for the green graves of your sires; God, and your native land!
author: Fitz-Greene Halleck

text: One flag, one land, one heart, one hand, One nation evermore!
author: Holmes

text: The noblest motive is the public good.
author: Virgil

text: The union of lakes, the union of lands, The union of States none can sever, The union of hearts, the union of hands, And the flag of our Union forever!
author: George P. Morris

text: I was born an American; I live an American; I shall die an American.
author: Daniel Webster

text: Our hearts, our hopes, are all with thee, Our hearts, our hopes, our prayers, our tears, Our faith triumphant o'er our fears, Are all with thee,--are all with thee!
author: Longfellow

text: How dear is fatherland to all noble hearts!
author: Voltaire

text: I could not live in peace if I put the shadow of a wilful sin between myself and God.
author: George Eliot

text: Five great enemies of peace inhabit with us--avarice, ambition, envy, anger and pride; if these were to be banished, we should infallibly enjoy perpetual peace.
author: Petrarch

text: There is nothing so likely to produce peace as to be well prepared to meet the enemy.
author: Washington

text: I never advocated war except as a means of peace.
author: U.S. Grant

text: There are interests by the sacrifice of which peace is too dearly purchased. One should never be at peace to the shame of his own soul--to the violation of his integrity or of his allegiance to God.
author: Chapin

text: Peace, above all things, is to be desired; but blood must sometimes be spilled to obtain it on equable and lasting terms.
author: Andrew Jackson

text: The block of granite, which was an obstacle in the pathway of the weak, becomes a stepping stone in the pathway of the strong.
author: Carlyle

text: I hold a doctrine, to which I owe not much, indeed, but all the little I ever had, namely, that with ordinary talent and extraordinary perseverance, all things are attainable.
author: Sir T.F. Buxton

text: Those who would attain to any marked degree of excellence in a chosen pursuit must work, and work hard for it, prince or peasant.
author: Bayard Taylor

text: Even in social life, it is persistency which attracts confidence, more than talents and accomplishments.
author: Whipple

text: A falling drop at last will carve a stone.
author: Lucretius

text: Attempt the end, and never stand to doubt; Nothing so hard but search will find it out.
author: Lovelace

text: It is interesting to notice how some minds seem almost to create themselves, springing up under every disadvantage, and working their solitary but irresistible way through a thousand obstacles.
author: Washington Irving

text: Press on! a better fate awaits thee.
author: Victor Hugo

text: Philosophy abounds more than philosophers, and learning more than learned men.
author: W.B. Clulow

text: Philosophy is the art and law of life, and it teaches us what to do in all cases, and, like good marksmen, to hit the white at any distance.
author: Seneca

text: A little philosophy inclineth men's minds to atheism; but depth in philosophy bringeth men's minds to religion.
author: Bacon

text: Whence? whither? why? how?--these questions cover all philosophy.
author: Joubert

text: Children are marvelously and intuitively correct physiognomists. The youngest of them exhibit this trait.
author: Bartol

text: As the language of the face is universal, so 'tis very comprehensive; no laconism can reach it; 'tis the short-hand of the mind, and crowds a great deal in a little room.
author: Jeremy Collier

text: Spite of Lavater, faces are oftentimes great lies. They are the paper money of society, for which, on demand, there frequently proves to be no gold in the human coffer.
author: F.G. Trafford

text: The scope of an intellect is not to be measured with a tape-string, or a character deciphered from the shape or length of a nose.
author: Bovee

text: People's opinions of themselves are legible in their countenances.
author: Jeremy Collier

text: We may learn by practice such things upon earth as shall be of use to us in heaven. Piety, unostentatious piety, is never out of place.
author: Chapin

text: Piety does not mean that a man should make a sour face about things, and refuse to enjoy in moderation what his Maker has given.
author: Carlyle

text: John Wesley quaintly observed that the road to heaven is a narrow path, not intended for wheels, and that to ride in a coach here and to go to heaven hereafter, was a happiness too much for man.
author: Beecher

text: We pity in others only those evils which we have ourselves experienced.
author: Rousseau

text: No beast so fierce but knows some touch of pity.
author: Shakespeare

text: O, brother man! fold to thy heart thy brother, where pity dwells, the peace of God is there.
author: Whittier

text: The world is full of love and pity. Had there been less suffering, there would have been less kindness.
author: Thackeray

text: Pity melts the mind to love.
author: Dryden

text: Let not the enjoyment of pleasures now within your grasp be carried to such excess as to incapacitate you from future repetition.
author: Seneca

text: The inward pleasure of imparting pleasure--that is the choicest of all.
author: Hawthorne

text: He who can at all times sacrifice pleasure to duty approaches sublimity.
author: Lavater

text: The end of pleasure is to support the offices of life, to relieve the fatigues of business, to reward a regular action, and to encourage the continuance.
author: Jeremy Collier

text: Choose such pleasures as recreate much and cost little.
author: Fuller

text: The pleasures of the world are deceitful; they promise more than they give. They trouble us in seeking them, they do not satisfy us when possessing them, and they make us despair in losing them.
author: Madame de Lambert

text: When the idea of any pleasure strikes your imagination, make a just computation between the duration of the pleasure and that of the repentance that is likely to follow it.
author: Epictetus

text: The seeds of repentance are sown in youth by pleasure, but the harvest is reaped in age by pain.
author: Colton

text: Pleasure, or wrong or rightly understood, Our greatest evil, or our greatest good.
author: Pope

text: Mental pleasures never cloy; unlike those of the body, they are increased by repetition, approved of by reflection, and strengthened by enjoyment.
author: Colton

text: I should rejoice if my pleasures were as pleasing to God as they are to myself.
author: Marguerite de Valois

text: We tire of those pleasures we take, but never of those we give.
author: J. Petit-Senn

text: Mistake not. Those pleasures are not pleasures that trouble the quiet and tranquillity of thy life.
author: Jeremy Taylor

text: True poetry, like the religious prompting itself, springs from the emotional side of a man's complex nature, and is ever in harmony with his highest intuitions and aspirations.
author: Epes Sargent

text: It is uninspired inspiration.
author: Henry Reed

text: Poetry is the blossom and the fragrance of all human knowledge, human thoughts, human passions, emotions, language.
author: Coleridge

text: Blessings be with them, and eternal praise, Who gave us nobler loves and nobler cares, The poets, who on earth have made us heirs Of truth and pure delight by heavenly lays!
author: Wordsworth

text: Poetry is the music of thought, conveyed to us in music of language.
author: Chatfield

text: He who finds elevated and lofty pleasures in the feeling of poetry is a true poet, though he has never composed a line of verse in his entire lifetime.
author: Madame Dudevant

text: Poetry is enthusiasm with wings of fire; it is the angel of high thoughts, that inspires us with the power of sacrifice.
author: Mazzini

text: Poetry is the record of the best and happiest moments of the happiest and best minds.
author: Shelley

text: Poetry is unfallen speech. Paradise knew no other, for no other would suffice to answer the need of those ecstatic days of innocence.
author: Abraham Coles

text: Poesy is of so subtle a spirit, that in the pouring out of one language into another it will evaporate.
author: Denham

text: Poetry is the child of enthusiasm.
author: Sigma

text: The art of poetry is to touch the passions, and its duty to lead them on the side of virtue.
author: Cowper

text: Poetry has been to me its own exceeding great reward; it has given me the habit of wishing to discover the good and beautiful in all that meets and surrounds me.
author: S.T. Coleridge

text: When the Divine Artist would produce a poem, He plants a germ of it in a human soul, and out of that soul the poem springs and grows as from the rose-tree the rose.
author: James A. Garfield

text: He who, in an enlightened and literary society, aspires to be a great poet, must first become a little child.
author: Macaulay

text: Poetry is the music of the soul, and, above all, of great and feeling souls.
author: Voltaire

text: There is as much difference between good poetry and fine verses, as between the smell of a flower-garden and of a perfumer's shop.
author: Hare

text: The world is full of poetry. The air is living with its spirit; and the waves dance to the music of its melodies, and sparkle in its brightness.
author: Percival

text: You will find poetry nowhere unless you bring some with you.
author: Joubert

text: Poetry is the robe, the royal apparel, in which truth asserts its divine origin.
author: Beecher

text: The poet may say or sing, not as things were, but as they ought to have been; but the historian must pen them, not as they ought to have been, but as they really were.
author: Cervantes

text: True politeness is perfect ease and freedom. It simply consists in treating others just as you love to be treated yourself.
author: Chesterfield

text: Politeness has been defined to be artificial good-nature; but we may affirm, with much greater propriety, that good-nature is natural politeness.
author: Stanislaus

text: Politeness is to goodness what words are to thoughts.
author: Joubert

text: Avoid all haste; calmness is an essential ingredient of politeness.
author: Alphonse Karr

text: There is no policy like politeness; and a good manner is the best thing in the world, either to get one a good name or to supply the want of it.
author: Lytton

text: There is no accomplishment so easy to acquire as politeness, and none more profitable.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: Fine manners are like personal beauty,--a letter of credit everywhere.
author: Bartol

text: Politeness induces morality. Serenity of manners requires serenity of mind.
author: Julia Ward Howe

text: As charity covers a multitude of sins before God, so does politeness before men.
author: Greville

text: When two goats met on a bridge which was too narrow to allow either to pass or return, the goat which lay down that the other might walk over it was a finer gentleman than Lord Chesterfield.
author: Cecil

text: Avoid popularity, if you would have peace.
author: Abraham Lincoln

text: Avoid popularity, it has many snares, and no real benefit.
author: William Penn

text: Seek not the favor of the multitude; it is seldom got by honest and lawful means. But seek the testimony of few; and number not voices, but weigh them.
author: Kant

text: Those men who are commended by everybody must be very extraordinary men; or, which is more probable, very inconsiderable men.
author: Lord Greville

text: Without frugality none can be rich, and with it very few would be poor.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: In one important respect a man is fortunate in being poor. His responsibility to God is so much the less.
author: Bovee

text: Morality and religion are but words to him who fishes in gutters for the means of sustaining life, and crouches behind barrels in the street for shelter from the cutting blasts of a winter night.
author: Horace Greeley

text: Poverty is the only burden which is not lightened by being shared with others.
author: Richter

text: We should not so much esteem our poverty as a misfortune, were it not that the world treats it so much as a crime.
author: Bovee

text: Poverty is the test of civility and the touchstone of friendship.
author: Hazlitt

text: That man is to be accounted poor, of whatever rank he be, and suffers the pains of poverty, whose expenses exceed his resources; and no man is, properly speaking, poor, but he.
author: Paley

text: That some of the indigent among us die of scanty food is undoubtedly true; but vastly more in this community die from eating too much than from eating too little.
author: Channing

text: Poverty is the only load which is the heavier the more loved ones there are to assist in supporting it.
author: Richter

text: Power will intoxicate the best hearts, as wine the strongest heads. No man is wise enough, nor good enough to be trusted with unlimited power.
author: Colton

text: The desire of power in excess caused the angels to fall.
author: Bacon

text: Even in war, moral power is to physical as three parts out of four.
author: Napoleon

text: The less power a man has, the more he likes to use it.
author: J. Petit-Senn

text: The greater a man is in power above others, the more he ought to excel them in virtue. None ought to govern who is not better than the governed.
author: Publius Syrus

text: Words of praise, indeed, are almost as necessary to warm a child into a genial life as acts of kindness and affection. Judicious praise is to children what the sun is to flowers.
author: Bovee

text: For if good were not praised more than ill, None would chuse goodness of his own free will.
author: Spenser

text: Praise has different effects, according to the mind it meets with; it makes a wise man modest, but a fool more arrogant, turning his weak brain giddy.
author: Feltham

text: Solid pudding against empty praise.
author: Pope

text: It is always esteemed the greatest mischief a man can do to those whom he loves, to raise men's expectations of them too high by undue and impertinent commendations.
author: Sprat

text: As the Greek said, "Many men know how to flatter, few men know how to praise.
author: Wendell Phillips

text: It is singular how impatient men are with overpraise of others, how patient of overpraise of themselves; and yet the one does them no injury, while the other may be their ruin.
author: Lowell

text: Good things should be praised.
author: Shakespeare

text: He hurts me most who lavishly commends.
author: Churchill

text: The love of praise, howe'er concealed by art, Reigns more or less and glows in every heart.
author: Young

text: Praise, like gold and diamonds, owes its value only to its scarcity. It becomes cheap as it becomes vulgar, and will no longer raise expectation or animate enterprise.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: He who praises you for what you have not, wishes to take from you what you have.
author: Manuel

text: Thou may'st be more prodigal of praise when thou writest a letter than when thou speakest in presence.
author: Fuller

text: Those who are greedy of praise prove that they are poor in merit.
author: Plutarch

text: What a person praises is perhaps a surer standard, even than what he condemns, of his own character, information and abilities.
author: Hare

text: Allow no man to be so free with you as to praise you to your face.
author: Steele

text: Whenever you commend, add your reasons for doing so; it is this which distinguishes the approbation of a man of sense from the flattery of sycophants and admiration of fools.
author: Steele

text: The first petition that we are to make to Almighty God is for a good conscience, the next for health of mind, and then of body.
author: Seneca

text: Prayers are heard in heaven very much in proportion to our faith. Little faith gets very great mercies, but great faith still greater.
author: Spurgeon

text: So much of our lives is celestial and divine as we spend in the exercise of prayer.
author: Hooker

text: Leave not off praying to God: for either praying will make thee leave off sinning; or continuing in sin will make thee desist from praying.
author: Fuller

text: Let our prayers, like the ancient sacrifices, ascend morning and evening; let our days begin and end with God.
author: Channing

text: Prayer is the soul's sincere desire, Uttered or unexpressed, The motion of a hidden fire That trembles in the breast.
author: Montgomery

text: If He prayed who was without sin, how much more it becometh a sinner to pray!
author: St. Cyprian

text: No man ever prayed heartily without learning something.
author: Emerson

text: He prayeth best who loveth best All things both great and small.
author: Coleridge

text: More things are wrought by prayer Than this world dreams of.
author: Tennyson

text: No man can hinder our private addresses to God; every man can build a chapel in his breast, himself the priest, his heart the sacrifice, and the earth he treads on the altar.
author: Jeremy Taylor

text: Holy beginning of a holy cause, When heroes, girt for freedom's combat, pause Before high Heaven, and, humble in their might, Call down its blessing on that coming fight.
author: Moore

text: It is so natural for a man to pray that no theory can prevent him from doing it.
author: James Freeman Clarke

text: The Lord's Prayer contains the sum total of religion and morals.
author: Wellington

text: It lightens the stroke to draw near to Him who handles the rod.
author: Washington Irving

text: In prayer it is better to have a heart without words than words without a heart.
author: Bunyan

text: Between the humble and contrite heart and the majesty of Heaven there are no barriers. The only password is prayer.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: Our prayer and God's mercy are like two buckets in a well; while the one ascends, the other descends.
author: Bishop Hopkins

text: Prayer is the voice of faith.
author: Horne

text: We should pray with as much earnestness as those who expect everything from God; we should act with as much energy as those who expect everything from themselves.
author: Colton

text: That is not the best sermon which makes the hearers go away talking to one another, and praising the speaker, but which makes them go away thoughtful and serious, and hastening to be alone.
author: Burnet

text: Be short in all religious exercises. Better leave the people longing than loathing.
author: Nathaniel Emmons

text: We must judge religious movements, not by the men who make them, but by the men they make.
author: Joseph Cook

text: The world looks at ministers out of the pulpit to know what they mean when in it.
author: Cecil

text: I preached as never sure to preach again, And as a dying man to dying men.
author: Baxter

text: It requires as much reflection and wisdom to know what is not to be put into a sermon as what is.
author: Cecil

text: To endeavor to move by the same discourse hearers who differ in age, sex, position and education is to attempt to open all locks with the same key.
author: J. Petit-Senn

text: Men of God have always, from time to time, walked among men, and made their commission felt in the heart and soul of the commonest hearer.
author: Emerson

text: I would not have preachers torment their hearers, and detain them with long and tedious preaching.
author: Luther

text: Precepts are the rules by which we ought to square our lives. When they are contracted into sentences, they strike the affections; whereas admonition is only blowing of the coal.
author: Seneca

text: He that lays down precepts for the government of our lives and moderating our passions obliges human nature, not only in the present, but in all succeeding generations.
author: Seneca

text: Precepts or maxims are of great weight; and a few useful ones at hand do more toward a happy life than whole volumes that we know not where to find.
author: Seneca

text: Prejudice is the child of ignorance.
author: Hazlitt

text: As those who believe in the visibility of ghosts can easily see them, so it is always easy to see repulsive qualities in those we despise and hate.
author: Frederick Douglass

text: Prejudice squints when it looks, and lies when it talks.
author: Duchess D'Abrantes

text: Human nature is so constituted that all see and judge better in the affairs of other men than in their own.
author: Terence

text: To all intents and purposes, he who will not open his eyes is, for the present, as blind as he who cannot.
author: South

text: The prejudices of ignorance are more easily removed than the prejudices of interest; the first are all blindly adopted, the second willfully preferred.
author: Bancroft

text: Prejudice is the twin of illiberality.
author: G.D. Prentice

text: Remember, when the judgment is weak the prejudice is strong.
author: Kane O'Hara

text: Prejudice and self-sufficiency naturally proceed from inexperience of the world and ignorance of mankind.
author: Addison

text: How immense to us appear the sins we have not committed.
author: Madame Necker

text: Busy not yourself in looking forward to the events of to-morrow; but whatever may be those of the days Providence may yet assign you neglect not to turn them to advantage.
author: Horace

text: He who neglects the present moment throws away all he has.
author: Schiller

text: Try to be happy in this present moment, and put not off being so to a time to come,--as though that time should be of another make from this, which has already come and is ours.
author: Fuller

text: Let us attend to the present, and as to the future we shall know how to manage when the occasion arrives.
author: Corneille

text: We may make our future by the best use of the present. There is no moment like the present.
author: Miss Edgeworth

text: Take all reasonable advantage of that which the present may offer you. It is the only time which is ours. Yesterday is buried forever, and to-morrow we may never see.
author: Victor Hugo

text: Every day is a gift I receive from Heaven; let us enjoy to-day that which it bestows on me. It belongs not more to the young than to me, and to-morrow belongs to no one.
author: Mancroix

text: What is really momentous and all-important with us is the present, by which the future is shaped and colored.
author: Whittier

text: In the long, fierce struggle for freedom of opinion, the press, like the Church, counted its martyrs by thousands.
author: James A. Garfield

text: Let it be impressed upon your minds, let it be instilled into your children, that the liberty of the press is the palladium of all the civil, political, and religious rights.
author: Junius

text: The liberty of the press is the true measure of all other liberty; for all freedom without this must be merely nominal.
author: Chatfield

text: Where there is much pretension, much has been borrowed: nature never pretends.
author: Lavater

text: When you see a man with a great deal of religion displayed in his shop window, you may depend upon it he keeps a very small stock of it within.
author: Spurgeon

text: True glory strikes root, and even extends itself; all false pretensions fall as do flowers, nor can anything feigned be lasting.
author: Cicero

text: It is no disgrace not to be able to do everything; but to undertake, or pretend to do, what you are not made for, is not only shameful, but extremely troublesome and vexatious.
author: Plutarch

text: He who gives himself airs of importance, exhibits the credentials of impotence.
author: Lavater

text: The desire of appearing clever often prevents our becoming so.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: Without the sovereign influence of God's extraordinary and immediate grace, men do very rarely put off all the trappings of their pride, till they who are about them put on their winding-sheet.
author: Clarendon

text: Pride and weakness are Siamese twins.
author: Lowell

text: Of all the causes that conspire to blind Man's erring judgment, and misguide the mind, What the weak head with strongest bias rules, Is pride, the never-failing vice of fools.
author: Pope

text: It is hardly possible to overvalue ourselves but by undervaluing our neighbors.
author: Clarendon

text: The sin of pride is the sin of sins; in which all subsequent sins are included, as in their germ; they are but the unfolding of this one.
author: Archbishop Trench

text: Some people are proud of their humility.
author: Beecher

text: Pride requires very costly food--its keeper's happiness.
author: Colton

text: Pride, of all others the most dangerous fault, Proceeds from want of sense, or want of thought.
author: Roscommon

text: If a man has a right to be proud of anything, it is of a good action done as it ought to be, without any base interest lurking at the bottom of it.
author: Sterne

text: There is this paradox in pride,--it makes some men ridiculous, but prevents others from becoming so.
author: Colton

text: Men say, "By pride the angels fell from heaven." By pride they reached a place from which they fell!
author: Joaquin Miller

text: Pride breakfasted with plenty, dined with poverty, and supped with infamy.
author: Franklin

text: When pride and presumption walk before, shame and loss follow very closely.
author: Louis Xi

text: How can there be pride in a contrite heart? Humility is the earliest fruit of religion.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: Pride is a vice, which pride itself inclines every man to find in others, and to overlook in himself.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: An avenging God closely follows the haughty.
author: Seneca

text: Charity feeds the poor, so does pride; charity builds an hospital, so does pride. In this they differ: charity gives her glory to God; pride takes her glory from man.
author: Quarles

text: The proud man is forsaken of God.
author: Plato

text: Faith in to-morrow, instead of Christ, is Satan's nurse for man's perdition.
author: Rev. Dr. Cheever

text: By the streets of "By and By" one arrives at the house of "Never.
author: Cervantes

text: By one delay after another they spin out their whole lives, till there's no more future left for them.
author: L'Estrange

text: Procrastination is the thief of time.
author: Young

text: For Yesterday was once To-morrow.
author: Persius

text: Never leave that till to-morrow which you can do to-day.
author: Franklin

text: Indulge in procrastination, and in time you will come to this, that because a thing ought to be done, therefore you can't do it.
author: Charles Buxton

text: He only is advancing in life whose heart is getting softer, whose blood warmer, whose brain quicker, whose spirit is entering into living peace.
author: Ruskin

text: Look up and not down; look forward and not back; look out and not in; and lend a hand.
author: E.E. Hale

text: I must do something to keep my thoughts fresh and growing. I dread nothing so much as falling into a rut and feeling myself becoming a fossil.
author: James A. Garfield

text: Humanity, in the aggregate, is progressing, and philanthropy looks forward hopefully.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: Human improvement is from within outwards.
author: Froude

text: An original sentence, a step forward, is worth more than all the centuries.
author: Emerson

text: Let us labor for that larger and larger comprehension of truth, that more and more thorough repudiation of error, which shall make the history of mankind a series of ascending developments.
author: Horace Mann

text: We are either progressing or retrograding all the while; there is no such thing as remaining stationary in this life.
author: James Freeman Clarke

text: A fresh mind keeps the body fresh. Take in the ideas of the day, drain off those of yesterday.
author: Lytton

text: Watch lest prosperity destroy generosity.
author: Beecher

text: Prosperity seems to be scarcely safe, unless it be mixed with a little adversity.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: The increase of a great number of citizens in prosperity is a necessary element to the security, and even to the existence, of a civilized people.
author: Buret

text: Prosperity is the touchstone of virtue; for it is less difficult to bear misfortunes than to remain uncorrupted by pleasure.
author: Tacitus

text: Prosperity demands of us more prudence and moderation than adversity.
author: Cicero

text: We must distinguish between felicity and prosperity; for prosperity leads often to ambition, and ambition to disappointment.
author: Landor

text: He that swells in prosperity will be sure to shrink in adversity.
author: Colton

text: Prosperity is very liable to bring pride among the other goods with which it endows an individual; it is then that prosperity costs too dear.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: Prosperity, in regard of our corrupt inclination to abuse the blessings of Almighty God, doth prove a thing dangerous to the soul of man.
author: Hooker

text: It is one of the worst effects of prosperity to make a man a vortex, instead of a fountain; so that, instead of throwing out, he learns only to draw in.
author: Beecher

text: Prosperity makes some friends and many enemies.
author: Vauvenargues

text: They who lie soft and warm in a rich estate seldom come to heat themselves at the altar.
author: South

text: Take care to be an economist in prosperity: there is no fear of your being one in adversity.
author: Zimmerman

text: The Providence of God is the great protector of our life and usefulness, and under the divine care we are perfectly safe from danger.
author: Spurgeon

text: I know not where His islands lift Their fronded palms in air; I only know I cannot drift Beyond His love and care.
author: Whittier

text: He who ruleth the raging of the sea, knows also how to check the designs of the ungodly. I submit myself with reverence to His Holy Will. O Abner, I fear my God, and I fear none but Him.
author: Racine

text: We must follow, not force Providence.
author: Shakespeare

text: Men are born with two eyes, but with one tongue, in order that they should see twice as much as they say.
author: Colton

text: Prudence is that virtue by which we discern what is proper to be done under the various circumstances of time and place.
author: Milton

text: When any great design thou dost intend, Think on the means, the manner, and the end.
author: Sir J. Denham

text: The prudence of the best heads is often defeated by the tenderness of the best of hearts.
author: Fielding

text: Prudence is a necessary ingredient in all the virtues, without which they degenerate into folly and excess.
author: Jeremy Collier

text: No other protection is wanting, provided you are under the guidance of prudence.
author: Juvenal

text: Prudence is not only the first in rank of the virtues political and moral, but she is the director and regulator, the standard of them all.
author: Burke

text: The rules of prudence, like the laws of the stone tables, are for the most part prohibitive. "Thou shalt not" is their characteristic formula.
author: Coleridge

text: I give it as my deliberate and solemn conviction that the individual who is habitually tardy in meeting an appointment, will never be respected or successful in life.
author: Rev. W. Fisk

text: I have always been a quarter of an hour before my time, and it has made a man of me.
author: Lord Nelson

text: Unfaithfulness in the keeping of an appointment is an act of clear dishonesty. You may as well borrow a person's money as his time.
author: Horace Mann

text: It is no use running; to set out betimes is the main point.
author: La Fontaine

text: I could never think well of a man's intellectual or moral character if he was habitually unfaithful to his appointments.
author: Emmons

text: Purity in person and in morals is true godliness.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: God be thanked that there are some in the world to whose hearts the barnacles will not cling.
author: J.G. Holland

text: While our hearts are pure, Our lives are happy and our peace is sure.
author: William Winter

text: Purity lives and derives its life solely from the Spirit of God.
author: Colton

text: Quarrels would never last long if the fault was only on one side.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: The quarrels of lovers are like summer storms; everything is more beautiful when they have passed.
author: Madame Necker

text: He that blows the coals in quarrels he has nothing to do with has no right to complain if the sparks fly in his face.
author: Franklin

text: Those who in quarrel interpose, Must often wipe a bloody nose.
author: Gay

text: Thrice is he arm'd that hath his quarrel just; And he but naked, though lock'd up in steel, Whose conscience with injustice is corrupted.
author: Shakespeare

text: Resolve to edge in a little reading every day, if it is but a single sentence. If you gain fifteen minutes a day, it will make itself felt at the end of the year.
author: Horace Mann

text: We never read without profit if with the pen or pencil in our hand we mark such ideas as strike us by their novelty, or correct those we already possess.
author: Zimmermann

text: We should accustom the mind to keep the best company by introducing it only to the best books.
author: Sydney Smith

text: Nothing, in truth, has such a tendency to weaken not only the powers of invention, but the intellectual powers in general, as a habit of extensive and various reading without reflection.
author: Dugald Stewart

text: Read, mark, learn, and inwardly digest.
author: Collect

text: Much reading is like much eating,--wholly useless without digestion.
author: South

text: Reason is the glory of human nature, and one of the chief eminences whereby we are raised above the beasts, in this lower world.
author: Dr. Watts

text: Let our reason, and not our senses, be the rule of our conduct; for reason will teach us to think wisely, to speak prudently, and to behave worthily.
author: Confucius

text: Though reason is not to be relied upon as universally sufficient to direct us what to do, yet it is generally to be relied upon and obeyed where it tells us what we are not to do.
author: South

text: He that will not reason is a bigot, he that cannot reason is a fool, and he that dares not reason is a slave.
author: Sir W. Drummond

text: Wise men are instructed by reason; men of less understanding, by experience; the most ignorant, by necessity; and beasts, by nature.
author: Cicero

text: When a man has not a good reason for doing a thing, he has one good reason for letting it alone.
author: Walter Scott

text: Good reasons must, of force, give place to better.
author: Shakespeare

text: There is a just Latin axiom, that he who seeks a reason for everything subverts reason.
author: Epes Sargent

text: God pardons like a mother who kisses the offence into everlasting forgetfulness.
author: Beecher

text: For when we came where lies the child We lost in other years, There above the little grave, Oh, there above the little grave, We kiss'd again with tears.
author: Tennyson

text: Refinement is the delicate aroma of Christianity.
author: Charlotte M. Yonge

text: That alone can be called true refinement which elevates the soul of man, purifying the manners by improving the intellect.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: Refinement that carries us away from our fellow-men is not God's refinement.
author: Beecher

text: Far better, and more cheerfully, I could dispense with some part of the downright necessaries of life, than with certain circumstances of elegance and propriety in the daily habits of using them.
author: De Quincey

text: He who reforms himself, has done more toward reforming the public, than a crowd of noisy, impotent patriots.
author: Lavater

text: Time yet serves, wherein you may redeem your tarnished honors, and restore yourselves into the good thoughts of the world again.
author: Shakespeare

text: Each year one vicious habit rooted out, in time might make the worst man good.
author: Franklin

text: Reform, like charity, must begin at home.
author: Carlyle

text: Whatever you dislike in another person take care to correct in yourself.
author: Sprat

text: He who reforms, God assists.
author: Cervantes

text: A wrong act followed by just regret and thoughtful caution to avoid like errors, makes a man better than he would have been if he had never fallen.
author: Horatio Seymour

text: A feeling of sadness and longing That is not akin to pain, And resembles sorrow only As the mist resembles the rain.
author: Longfellow

text: Of all sad words of tongue or pen, The saddest are these: "It might have been!
author: Whittier

text: A religion that never suffices to govern a man will never suffice to save him; that which does not sufficiently distinguish one from a wicked world will never distinguish him from a perishing world.
author: Howe

text: Religion crowns the statesman and the man, Sole source of public and of private peace.
author: Young

text: A true religious instinct never deprived man of one single joy; mournful faces and a sombre aspect are the conventional affectations of the weak-minded.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: The source of all good and of all comfort.
author: Burke

text: You may depend upon it, religion is, in its essence, the most gentlemanly thing in the world. It will _alone_ gentilize, if unmixed with cant; and I know nothing else that will _alone_.
author: S.T. Coleridge

text: Religion, if in heavenly truths attired, Needs only to be seen to be admired.
author: Cowper

text: Ah! what a divine religion might be found out if charity were really made the principle of it instead of faith.
author: Shelley

text: Leave the matter of religion to the family altar, the church, and the private school, supported entirely by private contributions; keep the Church and the State forever apart.
author: U.S. Grant

text: Religion is the mortar that binds society together; the granite pedestal of liberty; the strong backbone of the social system.
author: Guthrie

text: All belief which does not render more happy, more free, more loving, more active, more calm, is, I fear, an erroneous and superstitious belief.
author: Lavater

text: Never trust anybody not of sound religion, for he that is false to God can never be true to man.
author: Lord Burleigh

text: It is a great disgrace to religion, to imagine that it is an enemy to mirth and cheerfulness, and a severe exacter of pensive looks and solemn faces.
author: Walter Scott

text: Nowhere would there be consolation, if religion were not.
author: Jacobi

text: All who have been great and good without Christianity, would have been much greater and better with it.
author: Colton

text: Wonderful! that the Christian religion, which seems to have no other object than the felicity of another life, should also constitute the happiness of this.
author: Montesquieu

text: There are three modes of bearing the ills of life; by indifference, which is the most common; by philosophy, which is the most ostentatious; and by religion, which is the most effectual.
author: Colton

text: A house without family worship has neither foundation nor covering.
author: Mason

text: Religion is the best armor in the world, but the worst cloak.
author: Bunyan

text: I have lived long enough to know what I did not at one time believe--that no society can be upheld in happiness and honor without the sentiment of religion.
author: La Place

text: If we make religion our business, God will make it our blessedness.
author: H.G.J. Adam

text: The call to religion is not a call to be better than your fellows, but to be better than yourself. Religion is relative to the individual.
author: Beecher

text: Remembrance is the only paradise out of which we cannot be driven away.
author: Richter

text: You can't order remembrance out of the mind; and a wrong that was a wrong yesterday must be a wrong to-morrow.
author: Thackeray

text: I cannot but remember such things were That were most precious to me.
author: Shakespeare

text: Remorse is the punishment of crime; repentance, its expiation. The former appertains to a tormented conscience; the latter to a soul changed for the better.
author: Joubert

text: Remorse, the fatal egg by pleasure laid, In every bosom where her nest is made, Hatched by the beams of truth, denies him rest, And proves a raging scorpion in his breast.
author: Cowper

text: We can prostrate ourselves in the dust when we have committed a fault, but it is not best to remain there.
author: Chateaubriand

text: There is no man that is knowingly wicked but is guilty to himself; and there is no man that carries guilt about him but he receives a sting in his soul.
author: Tillotson

text: Repentance, without amendment, is like continually pumping without mending the leak.
author: Dilwyn

text: Repentance is but another name for aspiration.
author: Beecher

text: If you would be good, first believe that you are bad.
author: Epictetus

text: Repentance is a goddess and the preserver of those who have erred.
author: Julian

text: Let us be quick to repent of injuries while repentance may not be a barren anguish.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: Our hearts must not only be broken with sorrow, but be broken from sin, to constitute repentance.
author: Dewey

text: Our greatest glory consists not in never falling, but in rising every time we fall.
author: Goldsmith

text: Repentance is heart's sorrow, and a clear life ensuing.
author: Shakespeare

text: Power rests in tranquillity.
author: Cecil

text: Repose without stagnation is the state most favorable to happiness. "The great felicity of life," says Seneca, "is to be without perturbations.
author: Bovee

text: There is no mortal truly wise and restless at once; wisdom is the repose of minds.
author: Lavater

text: If you have a thrust to make at your friend's expense, do it gracefully, it is all the more effective. Some one says the reproach that is delivered with hat in hand is the most telling.
author: Haliburton

text: The severest punishment suffered by a sensitive mind, for injury inflicted upon another, is the consciousness of having done it.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: No reproach is like that we clothe in a smile, and present with a bow.
author: Lytton

text: Reproof is a medicine like mercury or opium; if it be improperly administered, it will do harm instead of good.
author: Horace Mann

text: He had such a gentle method of reproving their faults that they were not so much afraid as ashamed to repeat them.
author: Atterbury

text: Reprove thy friend privately; commend him publicly.
author: Solon

text: The way to gain a good reputation is to endeavor to be what you desire to appear.
author: Socrates

text: How many people live on the reputation of the reputation they might have made!
author: Holmes

text: Reputation is what men and women think of us; character is what God and angels know of us.
author: Thomas Paine

text: Resignation is the courage of Christian sorrow.
author: Professor Vinet

text: With a sigh for what we have not, we must be thankful for what we have, and leave to One wiser than ourselves the deeper problems of the human soul and of its discipline.
author: Gladstone

text: Let God do with me what He will, anything He will; and, whatever it be, it will be either heaven itself, or some beginning of it.
author: Mountford

text: Is it reasonable to take it ill, that anybody desires of us that which is their own? All we have is the Almighty's; and shall not God have his own when he calls for it?
author: William Penn

text: He only is a well-made man who has a good termination.
author: Emerson

text: Do not, for one repulse, forego the purpose That you resolved to effect.
author: Shakespeare

text: Rest is a fine medicine. Let your stomachs rest, ye dyspeptics; let your brain rest, you wearied and worried men of business; let your limbs rest, ye children of toil!
author: Carlyle

text: Absence of occupation is not rest. A mind quite vacant is a mind distress'd.
author: Cowper

text: Of all our loving Father's gifts I often wonder which is best, And cry: Dear God, the one that lifts Our soul from weariness to rest, The rest of silence--that is best.
author: Mary Clemmer

text: The word "rest" is not in my vocabulary.
author: Horace Greeley
