text: How much they err who, to their interest blind, slight the calm peace which from retirement flows!
author: Mrs. Tighe

text: Nature I'll court in her sequester'd haunts, By mountain, meadow, streamlet, grove or cell; Where the poised lark his evening ditty chaunts, And health, and peace, and contemplation dwell.
author: Smollett

text: O, blest retirement! friend to life's decline-- How blest is he who crowns, in shades like these, A youth of labor with an age of ease!
author: Goldsmith

text: Full many a flower is born to blush unseen, And waste its sweetness on the desert air.
author: Gray

text: Depart from the highway, and transplant thyself in some enclosed ground; for it is hard for a tree that stands by the wayside to keep her fruit till it be ripe.
author: St. Chrysostom

text: Riches exclude only one inconvenience,--that is, poverty.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: Great abundance of riches cannot of any man be both gathered and kept without sin.
author: Erasmus

text: Riches, honors, and pleasures are the sweets which destroy the mind's appetite for its heavenly food; poverty, disgrace, and pain are the bitters which restore it.
author: Bishop Horne

text: A man's true wealth is the good he does in this world.
author: Mohammed

text: Superfluity comes sooner by white hairs, but competency lives longer.
author: Shakespeare

text: No man can tell whether he is rich or poor by turning to his ledger. It is the heart that makes a man rich. He is rich or poor according to what he is, not according to what he has.
author: Beecher

text: Wealth is not his that has it, but his that enjoys it.
author: Franklin

text: Riches without charity are nothing worth. They are a blessing only to him who makes them a blessing to others.
author: Fielding

text: The Sunday is the core of our civilization, dedicated to thought and reverence. It invites to the noblest solitude and to the noblest society.
author: Emerson

text: Students of every age and kind, beware of secular study on the Lord's day.
author: Professor Miller

text: A world without a Sabbath would be like a man without a smile, like a summer without flowers, and like a homestead without a garden. It is the joyous day of the whole week.
author: Beecher

text: He who ordained the Sabbath loved the poor.
author: O.W. Holmes

text: If there is any person to whom you feel dislike, that is the person of whom you ought never to speak.
author: Cecil

text: There is a lust in man no charm can tame, Of loudly publishing his neighbor's shame;-- On eagle's wings immortal scandals fly, While virtuous actions are but born and die.
author: Ella Louisa Hervey

text: No one loves to tell of scandal except to him who loves to hear it. Learn, then, to rebuke and check the detracting tongue by showing that you do not listen to it with pleasure.
author: St. Jerome

text: Scepticism has never founded empires, established principles, or changed the world's heart. The great doers in history have always been men of faith.
author: Chapin

text: Scepticism is a barren coast, without a harbor or lighthouse.
author: Beecher

text: Freethinkers are generally those who never think at all.
author: Sterne

text: I know not any crime so great that a man could contrive to commit as poisoning the sources of eternal truth.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: The secret known to two is no longer a secret.
author: Ninon de Lenclos

text: A woman can keep one secret,--the secret of her age.
author: Voltaire

text: To tell your own secrets is generally folly, but that folly is without guilt; to communicate those with which we are intrusted is always treachery, and treachery for the most part combined with folly.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: To keep your secret is wisdom; but to expect others to keep it is folly.
author: Holmes

text: To whom you betray your secret you sell your liberty.
author: Franklin

text: He who trusts a secret to his servant makes his own man his master.
author: Dryden

text: What is the best government? That which teaches us to govern ourselves.
author: Goethe

text: He who reigns within himself, and rules passions, desires, and fears, is more than a king.
author: Milton

text: Real glory springs from the silent conquest of ourselves.
author: Thomson

text: He is a fool who cannot be angry: but he is a wise man who will not.
author: English Proverb

text: Self-denial is the quality of which Jesus Christ set us the example.
author: Ary Scheffer

text: Only the soul that with an overwhelming impulse and a perfect trust gives itself up forever to the life of other men, finds the delight and peace which such complete self-surrender has to give.
author: Phillips Brooks

text: Self-denial is a virtue of the highest quality, and he who has it not, and does not strive to acquire it, will never excel in anything.
author: Conybeare

text: The more a man denies himself the more he shall obtain from God.
author: Horace

text: Selfishness is that detestable vice which no one will forgive in others, and no one is without in himself.
author: Beecher

text: It is to be doubted whether he will ever find the way to heaven who desires to go thither alone.
author: Feltham

text: Take the selfishness out of this world and there would be more happiness than we should know what to do with.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: We erect the idol self, and not only wish others to worship, but worship ourselves.
author: Cecil

text: Be silent, or say something better than silence.
author: Pythagoras

text: God's poet is silence! His song is unspoken, And yet so profound, so loud, and so far, It fills you, it thrills you with measures unbroken, And as soft, and as fair, and as far as a star.
author: Joaquin Miller

text: Silence is the safest course for any man to adopt who distrusts himself.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: If thou desire to be held wise, be so wise as to hold thy tongue.
author: Quarles

text: As we must account for every idle word, so we must for every idle silence.
author: Franklin

text: Learn to hold thy tongue. Five words cost Zacharias forty weeks' silence.
author: Fuller

text: Silence is a virtue in those who are deficient in understanding.
author: Bouhours

text: Silence, when nothing need be said, is the eloquence of discretion.
author: Bovee

text: Silence does not always mark wisdom.
author: S.T. Coleridge

text: Suffer anything from man, rather than sin against God.
author: Sir Henry Vane

text: Let him that sows the serpent's teeth not hope to reap a joyous harvest. Every crime has, in the moment of its perpetration, its own avenging angel,--dark misgivings at the inmost heart.
author: Schiller

text: I could not live in peace if I put the shadow of a willful sin between myself and God.
author: George Eliot

text: Never let any man imagine that he can pursue a good end by evil means, without sinning against his own soul! Any other issue is doubtful; the evil effect on himself is certain.
author: Southey

text: Think not for wrongs like these unscourged to live; Long may ye sin, and long may Heaven forgive; But when ye least expect, in sorrow's day, Vengeance shall fall more heavy for delay.
author: Churchill

text: Sin is never at a stay; if we do not retreat from it, we shall advance in it; and the farther on we go, the more we have to come back.
author: Barrow

text: Other men's sins are before our eyes, our own are behind our back.
author: Seneca

text: Cast out thy Jonah--every sleeping and secure sin that brings a tempest upon thy ship, vexation to thy spirit.
author: Reynolds

text: I think you will find that people who honestly mean to be true really contradict themselves much more rarely than those who try to be "consistent.
author: Holmes

text: Private sincerity is a public welfare.
author: Bartol

text: I hope I shall always possess firmness and virtue enough to maintain, what I consider the most enviable of all titles, the character of an "honest man.
author: Washington

text: Sincerity is to speak as we think, to do as we pretend and profess, to perform and make good what we promise, and really to be what we would seem and appear to be.
author: Tillotson

text: Let us then be what we are, and speak what we think, and in all things keep ourselves loyal to truth, and the sacred professions of friendship.
author: Longfellow

text: When will talkers refrain from evil-speaking? When listeners refrain from evil-hearing.
author: Hare

text: Never throw mud. You may miss your mark, but you must have dirty hands.
author: Joseph Parker

text: Remember, when incited to slander, that it is only he among you who is without sin that may cast the first stone.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: Those men who carry about and who listen to accusations, should all be hanged, if so it could be at my decision--the carriers by their tongues, the listeners by their ears.
author: Plautus

text: Oh! many a shaft, at random sent, Finds mark the archer little meant; And many a word, at random spoken, May soothe or wound a heart that's broken.
author: Walter Scott

text: One hour's sleep before midnight is worth two after.
author: Fielding

text: God gives sleep to the bad, in order that the good may be undisturbed.
author: Saadi

text: Put off thy cares with thy clothes; so shall thy rest strengthen thy labor; and so shall thy labor sweeten thy rest.
author: Quarles

text: We sleep, but the loom of life never stops; and the pattern which was weaving when the sun went down is weaving when it comes up to-morrow.
author: Beecher

text: Heaven trims our lamps while we sleep.
author: Alcott

text: Sleep is a generous thief; he gives to vigor what he takes from time.
author: Elizabeth, Queen of Roumania

text: O sleep! it is a gentle thing, Beloved from pole to pole.
author: Coleridge

text: Society is ever ready to worship success, but rarely forgives failure.
author: Mme. Roland

text: Society is a troop of thinkers, and the best heads among them take the best places.
author: Emerson

text: Society is like a lawn, where every roughness is smoothed, every bramble eradicated, and where the eye is delighted by the smiling verdure of a velvet surface.
author: Washington Irving

text: Every man depends on the quantity of sense, wit, or good manners he brings into society for the reception he meets with in it.
author: Hazlitt

text: A man's reception depends upon his coat; his dismissal upon the wit he shows.
author: Beranger

text: Man in society is like a flow'r, Blown in its native bed. 'Tis there alone His faculties expanded in full bloom Shine out, there only reach their proper use.
author: Cowper

text: There is a sort of economy in Providence that one shall excel where another is defective, in order to make men more useful to each other, and mix them in society.
author: Addison

text: Society is composed of two great classes,--those who have more dinners than appetite, and those who have more appetite than dinners.
author: Chamfort

text: Nothing is impossible to the man that can will. Is that necessary? That shall be. This is the only law of success.
author: Mirabeau

text: Nothing succeeds so well as success.
author: Talleyrand

text: To know how to wait is the great secret of success.
author: De Maistre

text: The surest way not to fail is to determine to succeed.
author: Sheridan

text: 'Tis not in mortals to command success, But we'll do more, Sempronius; we'll deserve it.
author: Addison

text: If fortune wishes to make a man estimable, she gives him virtues; if she wishes to make him esteemed, she gives him success.
author: Joubert

text: Successful minds work like a gimlet,--to a single point.
author: Bovee

text: If you wish success in life, make perseverance your bosom friend, experience your wise counselor, caution your elder brother, and hope your guardian genius.
author: Addison

text: Success does not consist in never making blunders, but in never making the same one the second time.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: Bid abhorrence hiss it round the world.
author: Young

text: God has appointed us captains of this our bodily fort, which, without treason to that majesty, are never to be delivered over till they are demanded.
author: Sir P. Sidney

text: To die in order to avoid the pains of poverty, love, or anything that is disagreeable, is not the part of a brave man, but of a coward.
author: Aristotle

text: Suicide is not a remedy.
author: James A. Garfield

text: Beware of desperate steps. The darkest day, Live till to-morrow, will have pass'd away.
author: Cowper

text: The coward sneaks to death; the brave live on.
author: Dr. George Sewell

text: I think we cannot too strongly attack superstition, which is the disturber of society; nor too highly respect genuine religion, which is the support of it.
author: Rousseau

text: There is but one thing that can free a man from superstition, and that is belief. All history proves it. The most sceptical have ever been the most credulous.
author: George Macdonald

text: Religion worships God, while superstition profanes that worship.
author: Seneca

text: Superstition is the only religion of which base souls are capable.
author: Joubert

text: Superstition always inspires littleness, religion grandeur of mind; the superstitious raises beings inferior to himself to deities.
author: Lavater

text: The child taught to believe any occurrence a good or evil omen, or any day of the week lucky, hath a wide inroad made upon the soundness of his understanding.
author: Dr. Watts

text: Superstition is a senseless fear of God; religion, the pious worship of God.
author: Cicero

text: Superstition renders a man a fool, and scepticism makes him mad.
author: Fielding

text: I die adoring God, loving my friends, not hating my enemies, and detesting superstition.
author: Voltaire

text: To commiserate is sometimes more than to give; for money is external to a man's self, but he who bestows compassion communicates his own soul.
author: Mountford

text: A helping word to one in trouble is often like a switch on a railroad track,--but one inch between wreck and smooth-rolling prosperity.
author: Beecher

text: The greatest pleasures of which the human mind is susceptible are the pleasures of consciousness and sympathy.
author: Parke Godwin

text: What gem hath dropp'd and sparkles o'er his chain? The tear most sacred, shed for other's pain, That starts at once--bright--pure--from pity's mine, Already polish'd by the Hand Divine.
author: Byron

text: Sympathy is especially a Christian duty.
author: Spurgeon

text: Grant graciously what you cannot refuse safely, and conciliate those you cannot conquer.
author: Colton

text: Talent of the highest order, and such as is calculated to command admiration, may exist apart from wisdom.
author: Robert Hall

text: Talent without tact is only half talent.
author: Horace Greeley

text: Though we have two eyes, we are supplied with but one tongue. Draw your own moral.
author: Alphonse Karr

text: No great talker ever did any great thing yet, in this world.
author: Ouida

text: If you light upon an impertinent talker, that sticks to you like a bur, to the disappointment of your important occasions, deal freely with him, break off the discourse, and pursue your business.
author: Plutarch

text: What you keep by you, you may change and mend; But words once spoken can never be recalled.
author: Roscommon

text: Such as thy words are, such will thy affections be esteemed; and such will thy deeds as thy affections, and such thy life as thy deeds.
author: Socrates

text: But far more numerous was the herd of such, Who think too little, and who talk too much.
author: Dryden

text: He who indulges in liberty of speech, will hear things in return which he will not like.
author: Terence

text: The tongue is the instrument of the greatest good and the greatest evil that is done in the world.
author: Sir Walter Raleigh

text: He who seldom speaks, and with one calm well-timed word can strike dumb the loquacious, is a genius or a hero.
author: Lavater

text: Those who have few affairs to attend to are great speakers. The less men think, the more they talk.
author: Montesquieu

text: Speaking much is a sign of vanity; for he that is lavish in words, is a niggard in deed.
author: Sir Walter Raleigh

text: Tears of joy are the dew in which the sun of righteousness is mirrored.
author: Richter

text: The tear down childhood's cheek that flows, Is like the dewdrop on the rose; When next the summer breeze comes by, And waves the bush, the flower is dry.
author: Walter Scott

text: Shame on those breasts of stone that cannot melt in soft adoption of another's sorrow.
author: Aaron Hill

text: Tears may soothe the wounds they cannot heal.
author: Thomas Paine

text: Hide not thy tears; weep boldly, and be proud to give the flowing virtue manly way; it is nature's mark to know an honest heart by.
author: Aaron Hill

text: Tears are a good alterative, but a poor diet.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: The happiness and misery of men depend no less on temper than fortune.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: In vain he seeketh others to suppress, Who hath not learn'd himself first to subdue.
author: Spenser

text: Nothing leads more directly to the breach of charity, and to the injury and molestation of our fellow-creatures, than the indulgence of an ill temper.
author: Blair

text: A sunny temper gilds the edges of life's blackest cloud.
author: Guthrie

text: Temperance puts wood on the fire, meal in the barrel, flour in the tub, money in the purse, credit in the country, contentment in the house, clothes on the back, and vigor in the body.
author: Franklin

text: Fools! not to know how far an humble lot Exceeds abundance by injustice got; How health and temperance bless the rustic swain, While luxury destroys her pamper'd train.
author: Hesiod

text: Men live best on moderate means: Nature has dispensed to all men wherewithal to be happy, if mankind did but understand how to use her gifts.
author: Claudian

text: It is all nonsense about not being able to work without ale and cider and fermented liquors. Do lions and cart-horses drink ale?
author: Sydney Smith

text: Temperance is a bridle of gold; he who uses it rightly, is more like a god than a man.
author: Burton

text: Except thou desire to hasten thine end, take this for a general rule, that thou never add any artificial heat to thy body by wine or spice.
author: Sir Walter Raleigh

text: If you wish to keep the mind clear and the body healthy, abstain from all fermented liquors.
author: Sydney Smith

text: Though I look old, yet I am strong and lusty, for in my youth I never did apply hot and rebellious liquors in my blood.
author: Shakespeare

text: 'Tis one thing to be tempted, another thing to fall.
author: Shakespeare

text: Some temptations come to the industrious, but all temptations attack the idle.
author: Spurgeon

text: If men had only temptations to great sins, they would always be good; but the daily fight with little ones accustoms them to defeat.
author: Richter

text: Better shun the bait than struggle in the snare.
author: Dryden

text: Every temptation is an opportunity of our getting nearer to God.
author: J.Q. Adams

text: When a man resists sin on human motives only, he will not hold out long.
author: Bishop Wilson

text: But Satan now is wiser than of yore, And tempts by making rich, not making poor.
author: Pope

text: God is better served in resisting a temptation to evil than in many formal prayers.
author: William Penn

text: Those who have finished by making all others think with them, have usually been those who began by daring to think with themselves.
author: Colton

text: Our brains are seventy year clocks. The Angel of Life winds them up once for all, then closes the case, and gives the key into the hands of the Angel of the Resurrection.
author: Holmes

text: Thanks to the human heart by which we live, Thanks to its tenderness, its joys, and fears; To me the meanest flower that blows can give Thoughts that do often lie too deep for tears.
author: Wordsworth

text: In matters of conscience first thoughts are best, in matters of prudence last thoughts are best.
author: Robert Hall

text: Man thinks, and at once becomes the master of the beings that do not think.
author: Buffon

text: Nurture your mind with great thoughts. To believe in the heroic makes heroes.
author: Disraeli

text: One thought cannot awake without awakening others.
author: Marie Ebner-Eschenbach

text: Thought is the wind, knowledge the sail, and mankind the vessel.
author: Hare

text: Every pure thought is a glimpse of God.
author: C.A. Bartol

text: Speech is external thought, and thought internal speech.
author: Rivarol

text: Learning without thought is labor lost.
author: Confucius

text: The three foundations of thought: Perspicuity, amplitude and justness. The three ornaments of thought: Clearness, correctness and novelty.
author: Catherall

text: Time is like money; the less we have of it to spare, the further we make it go.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: Youth is not rich in time, it may be poor; Part with it as with money, sparing; pay No moment but in purchase of its worth; And what it's worth, ask death-beds; they can tell.
author: Young

text: Redeem the misspent time that's past, And live this day as 'twere thy last.
author: Ken

text: Time, the cradle of hope, but the grave of ambition, is the stern corrector of fools, but the salutary counselor of the wise, bringing all they dread to the one, and all they desire to the other.
author: Colton

text: Let me therefore live as if every moment were to be my last.
author: Seneca

text: The great rule of moral conduct is, next to God, to respect time.
author: Lavater

text: Lost, yesterday, somewhere between sunrise and sunset, two golden hours, each set with sixty diamond minutes. No reward is offered, for they are gone forever!
author: Horace Mann

text: As every thread of gold is valuable, so is every minute of time.
author: Mason

text: No person will have occasion to complain of the want of time, who never loses any.
author: Thomas Jefferson

text: Make use of time, if thou valuest eternity. Yesterday cannot be recalled; to-morrow cannot be assured; to-day only is thine, which, if thou procrastinatest, thou losest; which loss is lost forever.
author: Jeremy Taylor

text: He is a good time-server that improves the present for God's glory and his own salvation.
author: Thomas Fuller

text: Time flies over us, but leaves its shadow behind.
author: Hawthorne

text: Dost thou love life, then do not squander time, for that is the stuff life is made of.
author: Franklin

text: Let us be very gentle with our neighbors' failings, and forgive our friends their debts as we hope ourselves to be forgiven.
author: Thackeray

text: There is nothing to do with men but to love them; to contemplate their virtues with admiration, their faults with pity and forbearance, and their injuries with forgiveness.
author: Dewey

text: Tolerance is the only real test of civilization.
author: Arthur Helps

text: It requires far more of constraining love of Christ to love our cousins and neighbors as members of the heavenly family than to feel the heart warm to our suffering brethren in Tuscany and Madeira.
author: Elizabeth Charles

text: The religion that fosters intolerance needs another Christ to die for it.
author: Beecher

text: Has not God borne with you these many years? Be ye tolerant to others.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: A traveler without observation is a bird without wings.
author: Saadi

text: He who never leaves his country is full of prejudices.
author: Carlo Goldoni

text: Railway traveling is not traveling at all; it is merely being sent to a place, and very little different from becoming a parcel.
author: Ruskin

text: To roam giddily, and be everywhere but at home, such freedom doth a banishment become.
author: Donne

text: The use of traveling is to regulate imagination by reality, and instead of thinking how things may be, to see them as they are.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: He travels safest in the dark who travels lightest.
author: Cortes

text: Usually speaking, the worst-bred person in company is a young traveler just returned from abroad.
author: Swift

text: I think we may safely trust a good deal more than we do.
author: Thoreau

text: To be trusted is a greater compliment than to be loved.
author: George Macdonald

text: There is no right faith in believing what is true, unless we believe it because it is true.
author: Whately

text: Truth crushed to earth shall rise again; The eternal years of God are hers; But error, wounded, writhes with pain, And dies among his worshipers.
author: Bryant

text: Truth is simple, requiring neither study nor art.
author: Ammian

text: And all the people then shouted, and said, Great is truth, and mighty above all things.
author: Esdras

text: For truth has such a face and such a mien, As to be lov'd needs only to be seen.
author: Dryden

text: Without courage there cannot be truth, and without truth there can be no other virtue.
author: Walter Scott

text: Truth is violated by falsehood, and it may be equally outraged by silence.
author: Ammian

text: You need not tell all the truth, unless to those who have a right to know it; but let all you tell be truth.
author: Horace Mann

text: No pleasure is comparable to the standing upon the vantage-ground of truth.
author: Bacon

text: Nothing from man's hands, nor law, nor constitution, can be final. Truth alone is final.
author: Charles Sumner

text: The greatest friend of truth is time; her greatest enemy is prejudice; and her constant companion is humility.
author: Colton

text: I have seldom known any one who deserted truth in trifles that could be trusted in matters of importance.
author: Paley

text: Bodies are cleansed by water; the mind is purified by truth.
author: Horace Mann

text: Search for the truth is the noblest occupation of man; its publication, a duty.
author: Mme. de Stael

text: Truth is one; And, in all lands beneath the sun, Whoso hath eyes to see may see The tokens of its unity.
author: Whittier

text: Truth is the shortest and nearest way to our end, carrying us thither in a straight line.
author: Tillotson

text: The expression of truth is simplicity.
author: Seneca

text: What we have in us of the image of God is the love of truth and justice.
author: Demosthenes

text: The most unhappy of all men is he who believes himself to be so.
author: Henry Home

text: A perverse temper and fretful disposition will, wherever they prevail render any state of life whatsoever unhappy.
author: Cicero

text: What do people mean when they talk about unhappiness? It is not so much unhappiness as impatience that from time to time possesses men, and then they choose to call themselves miserable.
author: Goethe

text: All men are selfish, but the vain man is in love with himself. He admires, like the lover his adored one, everything which to others is indifferent.
author: Auerbach

text: There is no limit to the vanity of this world. Each spoke in the wheel thinks the whole strength of the wheel depends upon it.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: Every man has just as much vanity as he wants understanding.
author: Pope

text: Vanity is the natural weakness of an ambitious man, which exposes him to the secret scorn and derision of those he converses with, and ruins the character he is so industrious to advance by it.
author: Addison

text: Vanity is the foundation of the most ridiculous and contemptible vices--the vices of affectation and common lying.
author: Adam Smith

text: Vanity keeps persons in favor with themselves who are out of favor with all others.
author: Shakespeare

text: There is no restraining men's tongues or pens when charged with a little vanity.
author: Washington

text: Vanity makes men ridiculous, pride odious and ambition terrible.
author: Steele

text: It is our own vanity that makes the vanity of others intolerable to us.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: Vanity is a strange passion; rather than be out of a job it will brag of its vices.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: Extreme vanity sometimes hides under the garb of ultra modesty.
author: Mrs. Jameson

text: She neglects her heart who too closely studies her glass.
author: Lavater

text: Vice has more martyrs than virtue; and it often happens that men suffer more to be lost than to be saved.
author: Colton

text: The vicious obey their passions, as slaves do their masters.
author: Diogenes

text: A few vices are sufficient to darken many virtues.
author: Plutarch

text: Vice stings us, even in our pleasures, but virtue consoles us, even in our pains.
author: Colton

text: One sin another doth provoke.
author: Shakespeare

text: What maintains one vice would bring up two children.
author: Franklin

text: Vice and virtue chiefly imply the relation of our actions to men in this world; sin and holiness rather imply their relation to God and the other world.
author: Dr. Watts

text: He that has energy enough in his constitution to root out a vice should go a little farther, and try to plant in a virtue in its place, otherwise he will have his labor to renew.
author: Colton

text: Vices that are familiar we pardon, and only new ones reprehend.
author: Publius Syrus

text: This is the essential evil of vice: it debases a man.
author: Chapin

text: Vice is a monster of so frightful mien, As, to be hated, needs but to be seen; Yet seen too oft, familiar with her face, We first endure, then pity, then embrace.
author: Pope

text: Vicious actions are not hurtful because they are forbidden, but forbidden because they are hurtful.
author: Franklin

text: Virtue has many preachers, but few martyrs.
author: Helvetius

text: Virtue alone is sweet society, It keeps the key to all heroic hearts, And opens you a welcome in them all.
author: Emerson

text: The virtue of a man ought to be measured not by his extraordinary exertions, but by his every-day conduct.
author: Pascal

text: Virtue consisteth of three parts,--temperance, fortitude, and justice.
author: Epicurus

text: Virtue maketh men on the earth famous, in their graves illustrious, in the heavens immortal.
author: Child

text: When we pray for any virtue, we should cultivate the virtue as well as pray for it; the form of your prayers should be the rule of your life.
author: Jeremy Taylor

text: To be ambitious of true honor, of the true glory and perfection of our natures, is the very principle and incentive of virtue.
author: Sir P. Sidney

text: Virtue is everywhere the same, because it comes from God, while everything else is of men.
author: Voltaire

text: O let us still the secret joy partake, To follow virtue even for virtue's sake.
author: Pope

text: Well may your heart believe the truths I tell; 'Tis virtue makes the bliss where'er we dwell.
author: Collins

text: The only impregnable citadel of virtue is religion; for there is no bulwark of mere morality which some temptation may not overtop, or undermine and destroy.
author: Sir P. Sidney

text: Virtue is not to be considered in the light of mere innocence, or abstaining from harm; but as the exertion of our faculties in doing good.
author: Bishop Butler

text: What nothing earthly gives, or can destroy, The soul's calm sunshine, and the heart-felt joy, Is virtue's prize.
author: Pope

text: If you can be well without health, you can be happy without virtue.
author: Burke

text: Recommend to your children virtue; that alone can make happy, not gold.
author: Beethoven

text: I would be virtuous for my own sake, though nobody were to know it; as I would be clean for my own sake, though nobody were to see me.
author: Shaftesbury

text: Know then this truth, enough for man to know, Virtue alone is happiness below.
author: Pope

text: An effort made with ourselves for the good of others, with the intention of pleasing God alone.
author: Bernardin de St. Pierre

text: Good sense, good health, good conscience, and good fame,--all these belong to virtue, and all prove that virtue has a title to your love.
author: Cowper

text: Our virtues live upon our incomes; our vices consume our capital.
author: J. Petit-Senn

text: How few our real wants, and how vast our imaginary ones!
author: Lavater

text: Where necessity ends, curiosity begins; and no sooner are we supplied with everything that nature can command, than we sit down to contrive artificial appetites.
author: Dr. Johnson

text: Hundreds would never have known want if they had not first known waste.
author: Spurgeon

text: Every one is the poorer in proportion as he has more wants, and counts not what he has, but wishes only what he has not.
author: Manilius

text: If any one say that he has seen a just man in want of bread, I answer that it was in some place where there was no other just man.
author: St. Clement

text: It is not from nature, but from education and habits, that our wants are chiefly derived.
author: Fielding

text: War will never yield but to the principles of universal justice and love; and these have no sure root but in the religion of Jesus Christ.
author: Channing

text: Most of the debts of Europe represent condensed drops of blood.
author: Beecher

text: Battles are never the end of war; for the dead must be buried and the cost of the conflict must be paid.
author: James A. Garfield

text: A wise minister would rather preserve peace than gain a victory, because he knows that even the most successful war leaves nations generally more poor, always more profligate, than it found them.
author: Colton

text: War is a crime which involves all other crimes.
author: Brougham

text: To be prepared for war is one of the most effectual means of preserving peace.
author: Washington

text: War is a terrible trade; but in the cause that is righteous sweet is the smell of powder.
author: Longfellow

text: Although a soldier by profession, I have never felt any fondness for war, and I have never advocated it except as a means of peace.
author: U.S. Grant

text: I prefer the hardest terms of peace to the most just war.
author: C.J. Fox

text: Take my word for it, if you had seen but one day of war, you would pray to Almighty God that you might never see such a thing again.
author: Wellington

text: Wealth, after all, is a relative thing, since he that has little, and wants less, is richer than he that has much, but wants more.
author: Colton

text: Riches are gotten with pain, kept with care, and lost with grief. The cares of riches lie heavier upon a good man than the inconveniences of an honest poverty.
author: L'Estrange

text: Seek not proud wealth; but such as thou mayest get justly, use soberly, distribute cheerfully, and leave contentedly.
author: Bacon

text: Conscience and wealth are not always neighbors.
author: Massinger

text: It is far more easy to acquire a fortune like a knave than to expend it like a gentleman.
author: Colton

text: The way to wealth is as plain as the road to market. It depends chiefly on two words,--industry and frugality.
author: Franklin

text: It is only when the rich are sick, that they fully feel the impotence of wealth.
author: Colton

text: All other goods by fortune's hand are given, A wife is the peculiar gift of heaven.
author: Pope

text: She is not made to be the admiration of everybody, but the happiness of one.
author: Burke

text: Thy wife is a constellation of virtues, she's the moon, and thou art the man in the moon.
author: Congreve

text: For nothing lovelier can be found In woman, than to study household good, And good works in her husband to promote.
author: Milton

text: What is there in the vale of life Half so delightful as a wife; When friendship, love and peace combine To stamp the marriage-bond divine?
author: Cowper

text: It is more easy to be wise for others than for ourselves.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: The clouds may drop down titles and estates, both may seek us; but wisdom must be sought.
author: Young

text: True wisdom is to know what is best worth knowing, and to do what is best worth doing.
author: Humphreys

text: The fool is willing to pay for anything but wisdom. No man buys that of which he supposes himself to have an abundance already.
author: Simms

text: The first point of wisdom is to discern that which is false; the second, to know that which is true.
author: Lactantius

text: Wisdom is ofttimes nearer when we stoop Than when we soar.
author: Wordsworth

text: He who learns the rules of wisdom, without conforming to them in his life, is like a man who labored in his fields, but did not sow.
author: Saadi

text: Wisdom is to the mind what health is to the body.
author: La Rochefoucauld

text: As whole caravans may light their lamps from one candle without exhausting it, so myriads of tribes may gain wisdom from the great Book without impoverishing it.
author: Rabbi Ben-Azai

text: Wisdom consists not in seeing what is directly before us, but in discerning those things which may come to pass.
author: Terence

text: Wit, without wisdom, is salt without meat; and that is but a comfortless dish to set a hungry man down to.
author: Bishop Horne

text: Wit consists in assembling, and putting together with quickness, ideas in which can be found resemblance and congruity, by which to make up pleasant pictures and agreeable visions in the fancy.
author: Locke

text: There is many a man hath more hair than wit.
author: Shakespeare

text: You beat your pate, and fancy wit will come; Knock as you please, there's nobody at home.
author: Pope

text: Wit does not take the place of knowledge.
author: Vauvenargues

text: To place wit before good sense is to place the superfluous before the necessary.
author: M. de Montlosier

text: The world was sad!--the garden was a wild! And man, the hermit, sigh'd--till woman smiled.
author: Campbell

text: A young man rarely gets a better vision of himself than that which is reflected from a true woman's eyes; for God himself sits behind them.
author: J.G. Holland

text: O, if the loving, closed heart of a good woman should open before a man, how much controlled tenderness, how many veiled sacrifices and dumb virtues, would he see reposing therein?
author: Richter

text: Seek to be good, but aim not to be great; A woman's noblest station is retreat; Her fairest virtues fly from public sight; Domestic worth,--that shuns too strong a light.
author: Lord Lyttleton

text: A woman impudent and mannish grown Is not more loath'd than an effeminate man.
author: Shakespeare

text: What's a table richly spread, Without a woman at its head?
author: T. Wharton

text: O woman! in our hours of ease, Uncertain, coy, and hard to please, And variable as the shade By the light quivering aspen made; When pain and anguish wring the brow, A ministering angel thou!
author: Walter Scott

text: If the heart of a man is depress'd with cares, The mist is dispell'd when a woman appears.
author: Gay

text: Women are a new race, recreated since the world received Christianity.
author: Beecher

text: Not she with trait'rous kiss her Saviour stung, Not she denied him with unholy tongue; She, while apostles shrank, could danger brave, Last at his cross, and earliest at his grave.
author: E.S. Barrett

text: O loving woman, man's fulfillment, sweet, Completing him not otherwise complete! How void and useless the sad remnant left Were he of her, his nobler part, bereft.
author: Abraham Coles

text: American ladies are known abroad for two distinguishing traits (besides, possibly, their beauty and self-reliance), and these are their ill-health and their extravagant devotion to dress.
author: Abba Goold Woolson

text: To feel, to love, to suffer, to devote herself will always be the text of the life of women.
author: Balzac

text: All a woman has to do in this world is contained within the duties of a daughter, a sister, a wife and a mother.
author: Steele

text: I have always said it--nature meant to make woman its master-piece.
author: Lessing

text: The brain women never interest us like the heart women; white roses please less than red.
author: Holmes

text: There is nothing by which I have, through life, more profited than by the just observations, the good opinion, and the sincere and gentle encouragement of amiable and sensible women.
author: Romilly

text: My words fly up, my thoughts remain below, Words, without thoughts, never to Heaven go.
author: Shakespeare

text: We should be as careful of our words as of our actions, and as far from speaking ill as from doing ill.
author: Cicero

text: Immodest words admit of no defence, For want of decency is want of sense.
author: Earl of Roscommon

text: It is with a word as with an arrow: the arrow once loosed does not return to the bow; nor a word to the lips.
author: Abdel-Kader

text: Words are often seen hunting for an idea, but ideas are never seen hunting for words.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: I hate anything that occupies more space than it is worth. I hate to see a load of bandboxes go along the street, and I hate to see a parcel of big words without anything in them.
author: Hazlitt

text: Men who have much to say use the fewest words.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: What you keep by you you may change and mend; but words once spoken can never be recalled.
author: Roscommon

text: If you do not wish a man to do a thing, you had better get him to talk about it; for the more men talk, the more likely they are to do nothing else.
author: Carlyle

text: It would be well for us all, old and young, to remember that our words and actions, ay, and our thoughts also, are set upon never-stopping wheels, rolling on and on unto the pathway of eternity.
author: M.M. Brewster

text: Get work. Be sure it is better than what you work to get.
author: Mrs. Browning

text: Nothing is impossible to industry.
author: Periander

text: If you do not wish for His kingdom do not pray for it. But if you do you must do more than pray for it, you must work for it.
author: Ruskin

text: No man is born into the world whose work is not born with him. There is always work, and tools to work withal, for those who will; and blessed are the horny hands of toil.
author: Lowell

text: I doubt if hard work, steadily and regularly carried on, ever yet hurt anybody.
author: Lord Stanley

text: On bravely through the sunshine and the showers! Time hath his work to do, and we have ours.
author: Emerson

text: We enjoy ourselves only in our work, our doing; and our best doing is our best enjoyment.
author: Jacobi

text: The modern majesty consists in work. What a man can do is his greatest ornament, and he always consults his dignity by doing it.
author: Carlyle

text: To know the world, not love her, is thy point; She gives but little, nor that little long.
author: Young

text: The world is a fine thing to save, but a wretch to worship.
author: George Macdonald

text: The world is a bride superbly dressed; who weds her, for a dowry must pay his soul.
author: Hafiz

text: O who would trust this world, or prize what's in it, That gives and takes, and chops and changes, ev'ry minute?
author: Quarles

text: This world is God's world, after all.
author: Charles Kingsley

text: There is another and a better world.
author: Kotzebue

text: The only fence against the world is a thorough knowledge of it.
author: Locke

text: There is no knowledge for which so great a price is paid as a knowledge of the world; and no one ever became an adept in it except at the expense of a hardened or wounded heart.
author: Lady Blessington

text: A good man and a wise man may at times be angry with the world, at times grieved for it; but be sure no man was ever discontented with the world who did his duty in it.
author: Southey

text: I am glad to think I am not bound to make the world go right, but only to discover and to do, with cheerful heart, the work that God appoints.
author: Jean Ingelow

text: Everybody in this world wants watching, but nobody more than ourselves.
author: H.W. Shaw

text: O what a glory doth this world put on, For him who with a fervent heart goes forth, Under the bright and glorious sky, and looks On duties well performed and days well spent.
author: Longfellow

text: Trust not the world, for it never payeth that it promiseth.
author: St. Augustine

text: The act of divine worship is the inestimable privilege of man, the only created being who bows in humility and adoration.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: And so increase our love for Thee, That all our future days May one continued Sabbath be Of gratitude and praise.
author: Oke

text: Remember that God will not be mocked; that it is the heart of the worshiper which He regards. We are never safe till we love Him with our whole heart whom we pretend to worship.
author: Bishop Henshawe

text: The best way of worshiping God is in allaying the distress of the times and improving the condition of mankind.
author: Abulfazzi

text: The strength of opening manhood is never so well employed as in practicing subserviency to God's revealed will; it lends a grace and a beauty to religion, and produces an abundant harvest.
author: Bishop Mant

text: He who cares only for himself in youth will be a very niggard in manhood, and a wretched miser in old age.
author: J. Hawes

text: Unless a tree has borne blossoms in spring, you will vainly look for fruit on it in autumn.
author: Hare

text: The best rules to form a young man are, to talk little, to hear much, to reflect alone upon what has passed in company, to distrust one's own opinions, and value others' that deserve it.
author: Sir W. Temple

text: What we sow in youth we reap in age; the seed of the thistle always produces the thistle.
author: J.T. Fields

text: Girls we love for what they are; young men for what they promise to be.
author: Goethe

text: Reckless youth makes rueful age.
author: Franklin

text: Oh! the joy Of young ideas painted on the mind, In the warm glowing colors fancy spreads On objects not yet known, when all is new, And all is lovely.
author: Hannah More

text: In the lexicon of youth which fate reserves for a bright manhood, there is no such word as fail.
author: Lytton

text: If the world does improve on the whole, yet youth must always begin anew, and go through the stages of culture from the beginning.
author: Goethe

text: Young men think old men fools, and old men know young men to be so.
author: Dr. Metcalf

text: As I approve of a youth, that has something of the old man in him, so I am no less pleased with an old man, that has something of the youth.
author: Cicero

text: Youth is not the era of wisdom; let us therefore have due consideration.
author: Rivarol

text: Motives by excess reverse their very nature and instead of exciting, stun and stupefy the mind.
author: Coleridge

text: Nothing has wrought more prejudice to religion, or brought more disparagement upon truth, than boisterous and unseasonable zeal.
author: Barrow

text: Through zeal knowledge is gotten, through lack of zeal knowledge is lost; let a man who knows this double path of gain and loss thus place himself that knowledge may grow.
author: Buddha

text: Zealous men are ever displaying to you the strength of their belief, while judicious men are showing you the grounds of it.
author: Shenstone

text: He that does a base thing in zeal for his friend burns the golden thread that ties their hearts together.
author: Jeremy Taylor

text: Never let your zeal outrun your charity. The former is but human, the latter is divine.
author: Hosea Ballou

text: It is a coal from God's altar must kindle our fire; and without fire, true fire, no acceptable sacrifice.
author: William Penn

text: Violent zeal for truth has a hundred to one odds to be either petulancy, ambition, or pride.
author: Swift

text: Zeal without knowledge is like expedition to a man in the dark.
author: Newton

text: Zeal, unless it be rightly guided, when it endeavors the most busily to please God, forceth upon Him those unseasonable offices which please Him not.
author: Hooker

text: We do that in our zeal our calmer moments would be afraid to answer.
author: Scott
